subtopic: NATIONAL EXERCISE TO BE HELD ON MAY 5

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NATIONAL EXERCISE TO BE HELD ON MAY 5
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to make a statement on the national exercise in civil defence to be held on Friday, the purpose of which will be to test the emergency measures being developed by the federal and provincial governments and the municipalities.
This exercise was announced in March. At that time I said in a press statement that the purpose was to practise those emergency measures which are necessary for national survival and the continuity of government at all levels, to test the preparations that have been made and locate whatever gaps exist in planning and preparations.
The threat of a nuclear war is a constant companion of all who occupy positions of responsibility and trust, and because of that fact this government has put forward every effort on behalf of disarmament. I know there are some who say that the taking of any defensive preparations in the military or civil fields amounts to an admission of the inevitability of war. We do not take that view. Rather it is a recognition of the facts and realities that causes us to make preparations to the end that we shall be ready in the event that war should take place.
The survival operations which will take place on Friday are designed, with the co-operation of the provinces and municipalities, to assure that as far as possible many who otherwise would be certain victims might survive. The exercise will commence with the sounding of warning sirens now being operated by the army. There will be a broadcast explaining the nature and purpose of the exercise, and the public will be informed by continuing statements by radio and television that what is taking place is only an exercise and that there is no need to take alarm. Indeed, this morning I heard one of those messages put over C.B.C. advising people well in advance so that nothing in the nature of fear could possibly overtake any of our people.
In this exercise the public is not being asked, however, to participate as individuals or as families. The main operation will
take place at a central headquarters and at ten regional headquarters. The central headquarters will be located at Camp Petawawa, and at that location the government will be represented by the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Defence Production, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and possibly by one or two other ministers. I would appreciate it if Her Majesty's loyal opposition were to feel it could name one of its members to attend-I see a smile on the face of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who has always taken an interest in this regard-and perhaps members of the C.C.F. group would choose one of their number. They could join with the others at Camp Petawawa and see the operations at headquarters. There will be more than 150 officials from federal departments and agencies and from the army participating in the exercise at Petawawa.
At the regional centres which have been set up in connection with this particular exercise there will be representatives of the civilian side of the federal government, of provincial governments and of the army. In some cases ministers of provincial governments will be present. Senior army officers will be there to direct the work of the army in the field in connection with survival operations.
As I informed the house in August last, it is the intention in the event of war to designate in advance in each of the regional centres of government a senior representative of the federal government who will have authority to act on behalf of the federal government, particularly when communications with the national headquarters are interrupted or inadequate. Among the representatives of the government who will occupy the role of regional commissioners for the purpose of this exercise will be the Minister of Justice, who will do so at the centre at Nanaimo. The Associate Minister of National Defence will do so at Valcartier, Quebec; the parliamentary secretaries to the Prime Minister will perform this role at Camp Borden, Ontario, and at Fredericton, New Brunswick. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence will do so at Aldershot, where the Nova Scotia headquarters will be. In Nova Scotia, I might point out, the defence aspects of the arrangement are of particular importance. For the three

Civil Defence Exercise prairie provinces the parliamentary secretaries to the Ministers of National Revenue, Veterans Affairs and Agriculture will represent the government in the provinces in which they normally reside. The federal emergency measures regional officers for Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland will serve as acting regional commissioners at the centres in those two provinces.
This major exercise- will require the cooperative efforts of hundreds, if not thousands, of persons in municipal, provincial and federal civilian services. The co-operation shown has been most commendable. We have to be prepared, and without having had any previous experience with anything like it there is only one way in which these preparations can be made. That is in the manner we intend to follow on Friday, to substitute for an actual experience which all of us hope will not occur in our country or in any country in the world.

subtopic: NATIONAL EXERCISE TO BE HELD ON MAY 5
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the government we believe every effort should be made to work out a world wide disarmament agreement while there is yet time, but in the interim we believe it is only prudent that we should plan for any eventuality which might occur. In this respect we have stated our position, that in the event we have to live in a world where two great powers face each other over a period of years or decades, each with a capacity to wipe out the homeland of the other, we must take such precautions as we can by way of passive defence.
The Prime Minister has said that this exercise is being sponsored to determine the extent to which the planning to date is effective, and to determine the gaps that exist in the planning. We will permit the Prime Minister a bit of poetic licence this morning. We suspect that the situation now is that the gap exceeds, so far, the concrete results which have been achieved.
There is, we understand, a fall-out pamphlet which has been prepared and is now ready for distribution. We should have thought it logical that this pamphlet would have been distributed in advance of the exercise so the public at large might have had the opportunity to peruse it and to make such preparations, and give the matter such thought, as would seem fitting to them. We understand, however, that it will not be released until after the exercise on Friday, and until after the Prime Minister has appeared on the television news program that evening.
The interest of the hon. member for Essex East in these matters is well known. He has

contributed much to the public interest, not only in the matter of disarmament but also in regard to steps which must be taken to prepare ourselves for any eventuality in our homeland. He has put forward a number of worth-while suggestions, and we are glad to see that the government has taken some of them into consideration. Those of us on this side have also shown interest in extending the plan. You will recall the dismay we felt last summer, when we learned that even the basic equipment necessary for civil survival had not yet been acquired by the government. We understand that some crash programming has been done in the meantime, and we now look forward to learning something of the extent of it as a result of the exercise on Friday.
We are glad to hear that so many members of the government will be participating in this exercise. It is also nice to know that it is the government's belief that at least one member of each of the opposition parties should be spared in the event of an attack. That does not seem an unreasonable ratio having regard to the distribution of hon. members in the House of Commons at the present time. All we can say is that we hope the facilities provided for survival at these particular locations, which have been so designated, will be such that the government members, and indeed the opposition members who are privileged to be there, will themselves have the opportunity to survive and join the rest of us after the exercise is finished.

subtopic: NATIONAL EXERCISE TO BE HELD ON MAY 5
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say that members of this group do not wish to make any political capital out of the unfortunate necessities of our time. We appreciate the action of the Prime Minister in informing the house of the plan and of some of the details of this survival exercise. We are also glad to know that the public is being well informed in advance. This is very necessary in exercises of this kind. However, Mr. Speaker, I am certain that all hon. members, regardless of party, hope that the efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and all those associated with him in the United Nations and other gatherings to promote disarmament and work for peace will be crowned with success.
We in this group trust that this exercise will emphasize the necessity of increasing support for those who are doing their best under very difficult and frustrating international circumstances to make certain that the genuine article so far as survival is concerned will not be required.

subtopic: YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-EXPANSION OF DEVELOPMENT ROAD CONSTRUCTION

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-EXPANSION OF DEVELOPMENT ROAD CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to announce an expansion in the government policy for the construction of development roads in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. In doing so, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to welcome the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie) back to his place in the house. This is an occasion that he can help to celebrate with us.
Hon. members will recall that since 1958 the government of Canada has been actively engaged in the construction of roads to encourage prospecting for and the development of resources. This policy parallels in the territories the roads to resources program in the provinces. It has resulted in a thousand miles of development roads now in use or in some stage of construction in northern Canada. Practical experience has shown that to keep pace with the upsurge in northern development, and also to meet the diversified needs of the north, greater flexibility is required in road construction policy.
Under the new policy, four categories of development roads will be recognized. There are area development roads, which open up relatively undeveloped regions, and mine development roads, which serve an area where two or more mining companies have made substantial progress toward large scale production. These will be financed entirely by the federal government. Mine access roads which serve the property of one mining company capable of achieving production on a large enough scale to warrant federal assistance will be financed two thirds by the federal government and one third by the company concerned. This parallels similar arrangements existing in the provinces under the roads to resources program.
The former policy made no provision for tote roads or trails. These are low standard roads, built to provide temporary, seasonal, or year round access to the property of an individual company to bring in supplies or equipment for exploration, development or

Mr. Speaker, before I comment on the statement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, perhaps you would allow me to say a few words on a question of privilege, shall I say. In the past three months there were times when I had serious doubts of ever returning to this house. As hon. members know, cancer is a very emotional word. At the same time, I feel I have come through dark days and am now back in the house to stay for some time.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and through you the Prime Minister, the leader of my party, the leader of the C.C.F. and all other members of the house and their wives for what they have done for me and my family over the past few months. I am sure it had a great deal to do with my being here today.
At this time I should also like to express my sincere gratitude to my physician and surgeon, the staff of the Civic hospital and the doctors and staff of the Ontario cancer foundation. They treated me royally. They have done all they can and all I can do now is hope. I also want to express my sincere thanks to the staff of the House of Commons and members of the press gallery. I am sure that each and every one of my many friends in the house, along with my friends from coast to coast and the people of my riding, who sent me cards, letters and telegrams with words of encouragement and who offered their prayers for me have had a great deal to do with my recovery.
As a matter of fact, the other day I was feeling fairly good and I paid a visit to a woman I had met in the hospital a year ago. She told me about an old fellow of about 80 or 85 who lived near her. She said, "Everybody around here is praying for him to live and he should be dead". She said, "I told them to lay off". You know, this business of prayer snowballs. She said, "There is real power in prayer". Before I left she said to me, "Do you want me to put you on my list for a few prayers?" I did not refuse, of course; I said, "If you have that kind of faith and a man who should not be here is here, I would be happy to be on your list".

I also wish to thank my wife who spent many hours waiting at bus stops on her way to and from the hospital to visit me once or twice every day. I say again, ladies and gentlemen of the House of Commons, that I am glad to be back, and I want to thank each and every one of you from the bottom of my heart. I do not think words can express the feelings I have for each of you.
With regard to the statement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, I am sure the people of the north will be very happy to hear of the new policy on development roads which will provide more flexibility with respect to companies that find ore, in the building of roads to their properties. I am sure the people of the north will agree with me today when I say that I am very happy to have heard the statement of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

Mr. Chairman, when we reached five o'clock on Friday the hon. member for Athabasca was speaking. He has very kindly agreed to let me speak now in order to answer questions that were put to me by the hon. members who spoke that afternoon.
Before doing so, however, I should first like to clear up a misunderstanding which my opening remarks seem to have left in the minds of some of the hon. members who followed me in the debate, namely that I seem to believe that the economic picture is a rosy one and that all we have to do is continue in our present way of doing things and everything will work out for the best.
If I left that impression, Mr. Chairman, I am glad to be able to correct it now. In the speeches I have been making across the country since I became the minister of this department I have been stressing the fact that this country is up against the toughest competition for markets that we have faced since before the last war, and that we must do things a great deal differently than we are doing them at the present time if we are to successfully meet and overcome that competition.
This situation was brought about by the recovery of the countries of western Europe and Japan which were until recently customers of our products, and are now our toughest competitors. They have rebuilt their economies with the most modern plants and machinery, and are manufacturing products of good quality and design and selling at competitive prices. These products are displacing Canadian products, both in Canada and in the export market, in increasing quantities.
We have learned that there is no sentiment in the buying habits of the average Canadian

or of the citizen of any other country, for that matter. He or she will buy the best product at the lowest price, no matter where the goods are produced. If we want to make sales and thereby create jobs replacing the products that move off the retailers' shelves, we can do so only by producing products that people prefer to those offered by our competitors. They must be comparable in price, quality and design with what our competitors are offering for sale. If they are comparable, they will be sold in the markets of the world and in Canada, and Canadians will have jobs replacing them. If they are not comparable, they will be passed over and Canadians will not have jobs producing more of them.
Our trade commissioners told the businessmen who came to our trade promotion conference last fall that if they would come to their territories with samples of good quality and design, and willing to quote competitive prices, they would guarantee them sales. Surely you cannot get a better offer than that. Those who have made such selling trips and have taken good samples and quoted competitive prices, have made sales, and good sales; their plants have been kept busy and they have taken on extra staff to handle the extra business.
Sales have not materialized where quality, price and design were not competitive. There have also been many instances where the selling effort was not carried through by the company concerned. I am writing a personal letter of inquiry to the heads of all companies that have not followed through after prospective sales were initiated at the sales promotion conference, to ask why this has happened and urge that the selling effort be carried through.
Our trade commissioners will do everything humanly possible to promote sales, and they made that very clear to the businessmen who attended the conference. But the company must either send its salesman to the territory or, at the very least, send the samples and price lists that are needed for our trade commissioners to make the initial approach. As I have said, in all too many cases neither has been done.
In addition to putting forward a first class selling effort, it is up to our producers to turn out products that our salesmen can sell. The greatest salesman in the world cannot sell a product that is demonstrably inferior in design or quality, or obviously not worth the money that is asked for it. We must match what our competitors are offering the customers. I believe that the best way to make our products competitive is to follow the example of our toughest competitors, who brought themselves from the ashes of 90205-6-2714
Supply-Trade and Commerce war to peak prosperity and employment in just 15 short years. They did it by co-operation among management, labour and government, to bring costs down and improve quality and design.
It was to help bring about this kind of cooperation here in Canada that we recently called together the heads of the top 15 labour unions and the heads of the 15 largest management organizations. This group can have a great influence on those they represent, to bring about this desired result; but it will be up to the great mass of our people to decide that in their own best interests they should co-operate with their fellow Canadians to make our products competitive, and thus able to sell in the export and home market and provide jobs for our people. If they so decide, and get to work on the big job that lies ahead and give our salesmen products which will meet with customer acceptance around the world, then both our domestic and export sales will greatly increase.
The result can be full employment, and not the second highest but the highest standard of living in the world. But it is up to us, the people of Canada, to decide what we are willing to work for and whether we are willing to co-operate with each other to bring about the desired result. Surely we are willing to work as hard, and surely we are just as smart, as the people of western Europe who pulled themselves up by their own bootstraps in such spectacular fashion. I am confident that our people are more industrious, and are smarter, than the people of western Europe or any other part of the world, for that matter. The government has indicated clearly to our salesmen and our producers that we will work with them and help them in every possible and practical way in the big and very tough job that lies ahead. The time to start working together is now.
Some hon. members who spoke on Friday and in the debate last Monday and Tuesday expressed concern about the effects that the European economic community and the European free trade association would have on our trade with those countries. I share the concern of hon. members regarding the dangers to Canadian trade which could be inherent in the development of the European regional trading blocs, the Six and the Seven. Should the ultimate shape of these regional trading blocs eventually evolve in an inward-looking or protectionist trading form, then a backward step will have been taken in the progress of international trade. It is too soon yet to arrive at firm conclusions, although the final shape of our trading arrangements with western Europe is gradually taking recognizable form in the current

Supply-Trade and Commerce negotiations at Geneva. Nor do we yet know for certain what ultimate decision will be taken by the government of the United Kingdom concerning its future relationship with the European common market. This, too, is receiving and will continue to receive our closest attention in the weeks and months ahead.
These problems are under close and continuous study both in my department and interdepartmentally. Until our judgment dictates otherwise, this government will continue to follow a trading policy designed to expand trade with all countries to the greatest possible degree, and in so doing create the greatest possible employment for all Canadians.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I am glad to once again assure the committee that if at any time my department and I consider that it is in the best interests not only of those engaged in export trade but of the Canadian economy as a whole for Canada to join a trading bloc or association, I will recommend such a course of action to my colleagues.
I should now like to answer the questions which were asked of me last Friday. First of all, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo referred to our trade with the West Indies. I may say that the department is very conscious of the importance of our long standing ties with these territories whose economies are so complementary to our own. The newly emerging West Indian federation is our nearest neighbour in the commonwealth. In recent years it has taken about $40 million of Canadian goods annually, making it our fourth or fifth largest commonwealth market. The West Indies buy from us such staple fcommodities as flour, salt, cod and lumber, and a wide range of manufactured goods. Our main purchase from them is of course sugar, but we buy also such products as bauxite, petroleum, spices, cocoa and rum.
The department has given a great deal of attention to the West Indies in its trade promotion efforts. In January and February, 1959 we sponsored two highly successful trade fairs at Kingston, Jamaica, and Port-of-Spain, Trinidad. About 150 Canadian firms participated in one or other of these fairs, and it is estimated that they resulted in the creation of over $2 million of new export business. During our trade promotion conference last December the West Indies was one of the areas in which businessmen showed most interest. Of the 1,133 firms represented at the conference, 340 or almost one third expressed an interest in the West Indies. Our four trade officers in the area are now following up these interviews, and we hope there will be a significant increase in our export activity in that market.
We have been watching very closely the progress which is being made in the West Indies toward a customs union of the ten territories making up the federation. These territories have now reached broad agreement on plans for a customs union and will be submitting them soon to an intergovernmental conference for approval. When the West Indies have advanced sufficiently far with their own preparations for a customs union it will be necessary to revise the existing Canada-West Indies trade agreement of 1926, which provides for different margins of preference in the various territories. Meanwhile the department is proceeding with its own preparatory work so that it will be ready for this negotiation when the appropriate time arrives.
I was asked a question by the hon. member for Vancouver East regarding exports of sawn lumber to Japan. It may be that the figures he quoted apply to the individual exporter in British Columbia to whom he refers. However, export statistics show that Canadian shipments of sawn lumber to Japan have never reached 10 per cent of our total lumber exports over the past 35 years.
The chief reason for this is the fact that Japan has emerged as a leading world producer of lumber, ranking third only to the United States and Russia in total lumber output. Since the war Japanese lumber imports from all sources have been largely displaced by imports of logs and other round materials, principally from the Philippines. The total Japanese market for lumber has shown a marked decline in the post-war period and is currently running at some 40 million to 50 million board feet. By contrast, in the late 1920's Canadian lumber shipments alone to that market averaged nearly 200 million board feet.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm reviewed in detail the changing scene in regard to measurement throughout the world. Some countries which are large world traders have moved to the metric system and, additionally, others which are reaching increasing stature as traders have made the same decision. Any decision by Canada in this connection must, however, be governed by the situation as it exists. As Minister of Trade and Commerce I regret, as does the hon. member, those instances where Canadian manufacturers have lost specific orders by reason of the factor of measurement entering into design. We must face the facts of life, however. If precipitate action were taken to change to the metric system our losses in our major markets, the United Kingdom and the United States, would create far greater hardships. I believe that the hon. member recognized this in his remarks.

While it does not appear, I think all will appreciate that the metric system is, and for many years has been, a legal system in Canada. There is therefore no reason why manufacturers and exporters should not use that system should it meet particular needs. To go further at this time and legislate or encourage a change would have so many ramifications that it would be extremely difficult to recommend a course of action without a formal review.
I am impressed with the joint report of the British association for the advancement of science and the association of British chambers of commerce, which suggested that this question should be reviewed periodically by the board of trade in conjunction with industry and commerce and in conjunction with the commonwealth and the United States of America. The stated object of the review would be "to study jointly significant world developments in the usage of metric and non-metric standards. . I shall be glad to examine the situation to determine whether the time is now opportune to institute a similar review for Canada.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont asked me to explain what he thought was a conflict between the figures for the number of persons receiving unemployment benefits and the figures for the number of unemployed as given by the dominion bureau of statistics. The decision to use the figures we are now using was made after very careful study by the committee on unemployment statistics. I am sending across to the hon. member a copy of the report of that committee in the event that he may not be familiar with it. If, after he has had an opportunity to study it, he has any further questions, I shall be glad to speak to him about them and do anything I can to keep him informed.
During the discussion of my estimates on Friday the hon. member for Kootenay West asked several questions. He indicated that he was rather intrigued by the title of my department, namely trade and commerce, and suggested that he would like to have some explanation. I have looked up these words in dictionaries and find little difference in the definitions of the words "trade" and "commerce". As the department received its name many years before I was born, I am not sure just what was in the minds of those who named it originally.
The second question which the hon. member for Kootenay West asked was what is being done to develop co-operation among the various sectors of the economy to work toward improving our competitive position. In March the Minister of Labour and I called together
Supply-Trade and Commerce 15 leaders of business organizations and associations and 15 leaders of organized labour to discuss ways in which greater co-operation could be developed to increase the competitiveness of Canadian industry in both domestic and export markets. A very successful meeting was held, and the decision was made to establish a continuing tripartite committee in order to achieve greater cooperation.
Through the national productivity council, representatives of industry, labour, the general public and the government are also working together to develop programs to increase the competitiveness of Canadian industry. Similarly, the national design council will be made up of representatives of the various sectors of the economy. These steps have been taken so that all the various groups in the economy can unite their efforts and work together in improving the position of Canadian industry in markets both at home and abroad. I am sure that working together in this way we can achieve the same successful results as have the countries of Europe.
The hon. member for Kootenay West asked what efforts would be made by my department to achieve success in the export of various commodities to China and other Asiatic countries, apart from wheat. Our trade commissioner in Hong Kong has been very active in extending assistance to Canadian businessmen seeking contacts with the national trading corporations of the government of communist China which might be concerned with imports from Canada. As a result of his efforts, coupled with those of energetic Canadian businessmen, there has been quite a satisfactory improvement in the sale to communist China of our staple commodities. Exports to communist China for 1960 reached $8,700,000 as compared with $1,700,000 in the previous year.
As far as the other Asiatic countries are concerned, we have very active trade commissioner offices in Tokyo, Manila, Singapore, New Delhi, Bombay and Karachi. Our trade commissioners at these offices cover not only the country in which the office is located. Their territories also include contiguous countries and territories to which they travel and on which they report regularly. In this way our trade promotion efforts cover the whole of Asia.
The hon. member for Kootenay West also asked whether there had been any incidents involving Canadian subsidiaries refusing to accept orders from China or other Soviet bloc countries on instructions from the United States parent company, or because this was against the policy of the United States government. I can only say that there have been no such incidents brought to my attention.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The hon. gentleman's fifth question was, has the minister read of the proposals by Dr. Keenleyside and has he given them his careful study and attention? If so, will he inform the committee as to his opinion of their practical nature and of the possibility, as a result of the application of Dr. Keenleyside's proposals, of improving somewhat our position with respect to trade and commerce in Canada and consequently the unemployment situation.
Mr. Speaker, the proposals to which the hon. member refers have been drawn to my attention, and you may be assured that these, as well as other proposals, have been given consideration. Our policy is to have maximum trade in every commodity in every possible market to provide maximum employment for Canadians. The hon. member may be assured that any practical proposals which achieve these ends will appear in our trade policy program.
The hon. member also asked for some explanation of the work of the small business branch and for information about the type of inquiries received and the publicity material it has available. Two projects of some significance presently under way in the small business branch are: (1) the compilation of the results of a survey of Canadian universities which was made to determine what management educational courses are now available, the dates and duration of these courses, and the fees charged. When this com. pilation is completed the results will be forwarded to the universities for checking and, eventually, more widespread distribution. This is part of a plan for stimulating interest in work now being done in this field and for helping in the further promotion of such work where the demand exists. (2) "Taxation Statistics", published by the Department of National Revenue, is being examined in cooperation with that department with a view to producing a supplement which will provide financial statistics in greater industry and size detail for the benefit of small businesses.
Apart from the publication "Selling to the Canadian Government", recently published by the small business branch, and the other two publications just mentioned which, incidentally, are available to hon. members, the small business branch has been able to cover requests for general information on other subjects from existing publications of the Department of Trade and Commerce, including the dominion bureau of statistics, other federal and provincial departments and outside sources.
Requests for information through interviews, telephone calls and correspondence have numbered in the thousands. These


queries are for all types of information on government legislation and regulations as well as for sources of information on markets, financing, starting a new business, etc. There is little pattern to these requests, and there are no so-called typical examples. Many are answered by the small business branch; others are referred to appropriate sources in other departments and agencies. The branch performs a useful clearing house function in this respect.
Numerous business associations contact the small business branch about more general problems, particularly in the field of financing. The branch plays an important part in co-operation with other departments of government in the preparation of background information for the framing of legislation in the whole area of the financing of small business.
In reply to a request from the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador that I should take a sympathetic look at the fish industry in Canada, and particularly at the salt codfish industry, my department, through our fisheries division, has been very active in the field of trade promotion of Canadian fisheries products. Our trade commissioners around the globe report regularly on conditions in their respective areas for the information of the fishing industry. These market analyses are also followed up by on the spot appraisals by head office personnel who, in turn, maintain very close liaison with individual members of the trade. In addition, an interdepartmental fisheries trade committee, which includes senior officials in all government departments concerned with fisheries, meets at regular intervals to consider ways and means of assisting the fishing industry. When necessary, the manager of the Fisheries Council of Canada is invited to attend these meetings.
With respect to the salt cod industry, may I say that this matter is presently receiving very careful attention, particularly in view of the difficulties which the trade is encountering in marketing salt cod in Cuba. A fisheries expert of the department has visited different European markets twice in the past year, and a report of his findings was made recently to the Fisheries Council of Canada. I should add that the findings are very much more encouraging for the fresh frozen trade than for the salt trade. The position of the latter industry has been impaired by the difficulties which the industry is encountering in the Cuban market for salt cod. The situation is being kept under continuing scrutiny.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock on Friday afternoon I was speaking about the development of our great oil reserves in the Athabasca tar sands and their significance in the planning of Canada's future, and perhaps to the security of the western world. One of the essential steps in the development of this area would be the construction of a road between Fort McMurray and Edmonton.
You may wonder why I bring up the question of a road in respect to the Department of Trade and Commerce, but I do so because the provision of transportation facilities is very essential in keeping the cost of our materials down. If we cannot move them from the point of production to the markets we cannot compete in world trade. Today in our very complicated economy the various departments of government must have full co-operation. It is not good enough for the Department of Trade and Commerce to bring forward a plan to extend our trade unless it is done with the co-operation of the Department of Transport in order to develop roads, railways, air transportation facilities and shipping facilities. Therefore I do not hesitate today in bringing to the attention of the minister and the officials of his department, the suggestion that there must be co-operation in the provision of transportation facilities. The officials of the one department must co-operate with those of another. There must be co-operation between the Department of Transport and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in order to provide a road of some kind in this tremendous industrial field.
I was heartened to hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources say this morning that his department was ready to broaden the scope of the roads to resources program. The bottleneck seems to be that the provinces are either unable or unwilling to expend the money necessary to build roads across vast districts such as mine where populations are very small, and where there is no industrial development at the present time. Perhaps this is because the funds are not available at this time, but I am afraid if we wait for the Alberta provincial government to take this step we will be waiting a long time. I think we should stop being shy, and that the federal government should take the initiative in some of these fields. The north country cannot be developed unless we can get into it from the south. In the area from which I come there is a stretch of about 300 miles where there are no roads, railways or other facilities for transportation.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Our vision of the north certainly will not come to fruition unless we take positive steps. The people there are not afraid to take a chance on the future and they have not lost time. There is very little unemployment there. Everyone is working hard and there is room for literally hundreds of thousands of people. If we accept the challenge and take the initiative, showing them we are really behind them in developing this country, I am certain the people will act accordingly.
Assuming we have a road we will then need capital to develop the area. I would suggest that capital should be made available perhaps through the industrial bank to what I refer to as the "in between" businesses. We now have the power of assisting small businesses to the extent of $25,000 for the improvement of their capital program. It is perhaps possible for very large companies to look after their own financial needs. The government has also made it possible for quite large companies to get loans from the industrial bank in some cases to the extent of $500,000. That is a lot of money, but presumably the security behind such a company, in stocks, is such that our government is willing to make this money available. However, there are a vast number of Canadian businessmen in the in between range who need money to set up local industries throughout our local areas, and I would make a plea on their behalf, that this government seriously consider widening the powers of the industrial bank in order to assist these businessmen in the medium category by making available loans between $25,000 and $100,000.
I would further suggest that we should get behind the local automotive repair shops and the larger garages throughout eastern and western Canada, enabling them to expand and hire local labour to repair automobiles and farm machinery in the small towns and villages where the breakdowns occur. I would like to see loans made available-
