speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. member that I do not see how he can relate his present remarks to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The hon. member has been dealing with the development of national resources; with roads to resources which are a matter under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources; and he has mentioned the industrial bank, which is a matter under the Department of Finance. I doubt that his remarks can be related to the items under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I have had personal experience in attempting to raise loans

Supply-Trade and Commerce through the industrial bank for trade purposes, as a result of which I would suggest close co-operation is required with the Department of Trade and Commerce. I would go so far as to suggest that the industrial bank should either be controlled by the Department of Trade and Commerce or that at least there should be high ranking liaison officers operating between that bank and the Department of Trade and Commerce so that when an individual makes an application to the bank for a loan for trade purposes he does not meet with the blank statement that it is a matter to be directed to the Department of Finance. There must be co-operation between the senior officials of the various departments so that, during the hearing of an application for a loan, officials of the different departments could sit in to give advice and make a joint effort to assist these medium businessmen. We will never have liaison of the kind I am referring to, which I feel is essential, because money alone is not enough, if we do not take a step in that direction. The bottleneck in Canadian development has always been finance. It is very difficult to discuss transportation, trade or co-operation with the provinces for the development of our resources unless you concentrate upon and discuss the sacred cow of finance.

I should like to ask the minister to comment on the foreign service personnel. As I mentioned the other day, I understand that some of his best and most highly trained men are leaving the service to take over managerial posts in private industry. In view of what the minister said only today with respect to the problems facing Canada in the competitive field, and in view of what I read in the press a couple of days ago and the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that he thinks we have been missing great opportunities to trade with Asia, it should be easily understood and recognized at this time that perhaps more than ever we need trained foreign service officers.
I believe we have been losing some because of their wages. I admit I was rather amazed, on looking over the details on page 509 of the estimates book, to find that we have 30 foreign service officers whose annual wages are between $4,380 and $5,880; 23 between $5,940 and $7,140; and so on. I would imagine that any civil servant in the foreign service is a relatively well trained officer. There are four classifications before you get to the salary range of $9,800. If this is the range of salaries, I can well understand why we are losing these experienced men. It is of the utmost importance that they be retained in the service. Can the minister tell us what is the

situation with respect to the retention of these trained men and whether or not it is the money factor which is driving them away?

I am glad to comment on that, Mr. Chairman. Morale among the trade commissioners is very high indeed, as I am pleased to say it is among the personnel of the department generally. It is inevitable that good men in the government service are lured away from time to time by business and industry. It is very regrettable that this is so because, as the hon. member said, in that way we lose very valuable men. We have lost two trade commissioners. I regret very much that this has happened. However, it is two out of several hundred people in that category employed by the department, all of whom are very able. Therefore the percentage of loss is not great. We would certainly prefer not to lose any. I agree with everything the hon. member says. It is to be regretted that any of these men are, as he said, lured away by business, but it always happens in the government service where we are limited in the amount of salaries that we can pay. When a man is outstanding he is often attracted away by a salary that the government cannot pay.
Once again I mention the fact that these are only two out of several hundred employees of that category. The morale in the department is very high and I think we loose relatively few of our good men.

Mr. Chairman, Canada's
trouble in the matter of trade is that we buy too much abroad; we buy more than we sell. In 1959, Canada bought $369 million worth more abroad than she sold there. Besides this, there is an amount of something over $1 billion that the minister did not mention the other day that we have to meet in the balance of payments. This amount is made up of such things as the expenses of people travelling abroad and the amount that we have to pay in interest and dividends on foreign investments in Canada, and so on. Our total adverse balance last year was very close to $1.5 billion. If a merchant continues to buy more than he sells he will soon go bankrupt and out of business unless somebody lends him money, and this is precisely what has happened in Canada. The United States investors mainly have put up the difference. As Canadian money has poured forth to pay for purchases abroad investors from abroad have sent money into Canada and have made up the $1.5 billion difference in 1959.
Over the last number of years our imports have gone up relatively more than our exports, and we have a deficit balance of trade. Certainly in the last three or four years there has been a relative slow-down in our

trade. However, I will say that in 1960 there was some improvement in our exports. They were up, as the minister said, some 5 per cent. Our deficit on merchandise account amounted to something under $100 million, I think about $97 million. This improvement was brought about by two things, by some decrease in the amount of our imports and also by an increase in exports mainly to Great Britain, to countries of the European common market and to Japan. This is largely offset by the decrease in our exports to the United States of 4.6 per cent.
For the last three months, the minister said, there has been a decrease of 17 per cent, compared with a year ago, in our total exports to the United States and 3 per cent in the total exports over all. According to the Globe and Mail of April 29, Canada's February trade deficit was $24.3 million. Our exports were down 13.5 per cent over all and to the United States by 19 per cent. It would seem to me that probably the Prime Minister has his proposal of the 15 per cent switch of trade almost within his grasp, except that our exports to the United Kingdom would need to go up 50 per cent from here in order to compensate for the 15 per cent cut-back in our exports to the United States.
During the course of last year I read several articles in the press, and I read some in the British press as well, complaining that Canada was not buying as much from Britain as we were selling there. I do not think we should try to switch any trade. We should not try to cut down our exports to any country. I was glad to hear the minister say today that he would try to sell in all parts of the world. At the time that the 15 per cent proposal appeared in the press we certainly got a bad press in the United States.
In 1957 when the Americans cut back the importation of crude oil into that country by exactly 15 per cent our oil exporters certainly were hurt, particularly those exporting oil to the northwestern United States. I have often wondered whether the Americans did not accommodate the Prime Minister by cutting back oil importations by 15 per cent.
A few years ago Canada was the third trading nation in the world and on a per capita basis the highest. Today we are the fifth trading nation in the world. In spite of the increases the minister told us about the other day, Canada is losing out relatively in world trade. According to the international financial statistics on world trade for April 1, 1961, Canada in the first nine months of 1960 had an increase of exports of 2.3 per cent compared with an increase in world exports of 9.3 per cent so that, relatively speaking, Canada is slipping in world trade.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
The minister himself has said that 25 per cent of all Canadians depend on world trade for their jobs. Therefore there is a direct relationship between world trade and employment in this country. Unemployment at the present time stands at something over 11.1 per cent of our working force and in this respect we are worse off than any other country in the western free world. There is only one other country that comes anywhere near us in that regard and that is Italy with unemployment amounting to 9 per cent of its working force.

Where did you get your
figures?

After all, our production costs are the deciding factor in the selling of our products in foreign markets. Anything that increases our costs will tend to keep us out of foreign markets. The fiscal policy of the government has contributed to higher production costs because we tax industry more than we did before. Our fiscal policy has also pushed up interest rates and money costs our producers more than it did before 1957. Industries also pay local and provincial taxes and we know that local and provincial taxes have gone up because of the increase in interest rates.
I want to commend the minister for his efforts in trying to sell our products on foreign markets. I wish him well but I think he as a member of the cabinet could do something about keeping down governmental costs in this country and certainly he could see that they do not rise more because of further financial manoeuvring. I should like him to remember that we have the highest unemployment in the western world and that we have lost our position in world trade, having slipped back at least one position from the time of the last administration. The minister should also remember that our per capita production is down nearly 1 per cent. We hear much about the European trading blocs such as the European common market or inner six and the European free trade area or outer seven. In the case of the inner six where free or freer trade is in operation between these countries, there has been a great increase in trade. According to the last figures I saw there had been an increase of 28 to 30 per cent in trade between them.
The United Kingdom is most likely to join one or other of these free trade areas, and I hope our ministers will cease issuing threats to the United Kingdom and the members of the European common market with regard to any steps they may take in this respect. I know that the Minister of Finance has denied these threats, but I have here a clipping from the Toronto Telegram of September 29, 1960,

Supply-Trade and Commerce a newspaper which is never unfavourable to the government. The heading of the article is, "Keep Out or Else, Fleming Warns United Kingdom". It is a dispatch from London, England, and the first paragraph reads as follows:
Canadian finance minister, Donald Fleming, today warned that any discrimination against Canadian goods resulting from Britain's entry into the European common market might be answered in kind by Canada.
If that is not a threat, I do not know what a threat is. I have several more clippings here concerning threats to Great Britain and to members of the European common market, even one or two by the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself. I do not think these threats do any good. They only tend to alienate our friends abroad. There was an article in the Financial Post of December 10 last by Mr. Clive Baxter headed, "In Europe They Say That Canada Overrates Her Own Importance". He quotes Mr. Hugo de Grood, head of the North American division in the directorate general for external relations at European common market headquarters, and also quotes others. Among the quotations was the following:
You are going to have to live with us in the future, and to withdraw into an angry protective shell can only mean worse and worse trouble for your economy.
All I can say about that is that the author of those words must have heard one of the angry tirades of the Minister of Finance such as we often hear in the house and have long since learned to discount. With reference to the speech of the Minister of Finance the writer said:
It is not encouraging to report, but impossible to ignore, that the speech seemed to worry nobody in Brussels.
He has reference to the headquarters of the European common market. Finally, in an interview Mr. de Grood had this to say:
It seems to us that Canada overrates its own importance these days. We want to trade with you, but you must understand that if necessary we can get along without you.
The European countries are going to enter these trading blocs anyway so I do not think our ministers should be making public statements that only alienate them. Mr. George de Young, chairman of the productivity council, speaking in Toronto on Tuesday said in effect that all nations and blocs of nations are putting forth a highly organized effort to increase the economic status of their people. He also said that we are suffering as a result of this and that in Canada and the United States we have to get over the idea that we have a technological and economic superiority because in fact we do not possess it. I think there is an awakening among all groups in our population to the

fact that we must become more competitive in world markets if we are to survive. We must have the co-operation of all groups in the community. Above all, we must have the co-operation of the government to keep costs down.
I remember that, a year or so ago when we had before us a bill increasing our subscription to the monetary fund and to the international bank, at that time I called the attention of the house to the fact that this bank would be lending money to develop industries in some of these countries at a rate lower than that at which our industries could borrow money in this country, and I said I thought that was unfair competition. That situation has come about. I have inquired about the interest rate that has been charged by the international monetary fund. I find that some of the industrialists in some of these countries have been able to build plants and to get new machinery and that they have been able to do that with money obtained at a cheaper rate than that at which our industrialists have been able to borrow money in Canada. They make products that come here to Canada in competition with our own domestic products.
I just want to refer briefly to agricultural exports. I was interested in reading lately that in the fiscal year 1959-60 our agricultural exports to the United States stood at $184 million, down 24 per cent from 1959 and 30 per cent below the 1952-54 average. Many fruit and vegetable growers in my part of the country are greatly interested in the marketing of their products. According to the November, 1960 issue of The Grower reference is made to our dealing with the United States in respect to fruits and vegetables under the heading "Imports are Up, Exports are Down". In the first six months of 1960 our imports of fruits and vegetables were up by $9 million to $76.3 million, indicating a figure of $150 million for the full year. At the same time our exports to the United States in fruit and vegetables were down by $500,000 in six months or by $1 million for a full year to about $13 million in fruits and vegetables alone. Therefore there is a net cost to Canada of at least $135 million in balance of payments. This is enough to wipe out our whole trade merchandise deficit and to have a surplus left over.
The hon. member for Vancouver East some time ago was referring to the deterioration of the fruit and vegetable production in British Columbia. At that time he said that a number of United States interests have come over and bought up certain of their processing plants and have cut down the opportunity for their producers in that part of the country to

market their fruit as well as they did previously. That same thing happened in the Niagara district some two or three years ago. I heard about some United States interests coming over and buying some of the canning factories with the result that thereafter the fruit and vegetable growers had some difficulty in getting rid of their products. I think that the two senior governments-I refer to the federal government and the provincial governments-should co-operate in helping these producers to provide facilities for the processing of their fruits and vegetables in Canada. If Canadians could use more of these fruits and vegetables and could import less, it would help the Minister of Finance in his balance of payments.
I have here a list of imports of small fruits for the last four years. I find, for instance, that imports of apples hold about the same; strawberry imports are down somewhat but in respect of most of the other fruits imports have gone up markedly. That statement applies to apricots, peaches, plums, cherries and so on. Let us consider the situation with regard to peaches alone. Imports of peaches in 1957 amounted to 423,000 bushels while in 1960 the figure stood at 945,000 bushels or over double. No doubt in some years there is a poor crop but, generally speaking, if you look over this list of fruit imports, you will find that they are all going up year after year.
Our farmers must be able to sell their fruit and vegetables when they produce them. They have high local taxes. Their costs of production are high and their cost of living is high. The people of Canada should endeavour to help them because we shall at the same time be helping ourselves in that we shall be cutting down the balance of payments.
I often see in the press some reference to United States companies moving to Canada, taking as much as possible out of Canada and giving as little as possible in return. This is not true in my part of the country. One United States company I have in mind is the Atlas Steel Company. The Atlas Steel Company came to Welland some years ago. It was brought there by Mr. Davis who moved to Canada and made Canada his home. Several of the chief executives have taken an active part in local affairs and they contribute much to the industrial and cultural life of their adopted country and community.
Two men in this respect are outstanding in my district, and they are two among others. I will mention their names. One is Mr. Arthur Schmon, president of the Ontario Paper Company at Thorold and Baie
Supply-Trade and Commerce Comeau. The other is Mr. George de Young, president of Atlas Steel Company in Welland. Both these men were born in the United States and they chose to make Canada their home. They have given leadership in some aspects of community and national life as well as being leaders in their particular industries.
I am sure the hon. member for Lincoln would agree with me that Mr. Schmon, among other things, has been instrumental in providing the most modern hospitalization in our area. We all know that Mr. George de Young was lately selected to be chairman of the productivity council. I am sure he will devote to this activity the same zeal and determination to make a success of it as he has devoted to the production of stainless steel and other products in Welland.

In this debate on trade and commerce I wish to advocate increased trade on the part of Canadian businessmen with businessmen in the republic of China in Taiwan or Formosa as it is commonly called in the west. Before I get into that subject I wish to commend my old friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the initiative, drive and enthusiasm which he has displayed in the discharge of his extremely important duties. The reason that I think we should promote greater trade between our country and this country in the Pacific is that, in my opinion, such trade would be beneficial in a material way to both countries and would lead to a greater understanding between Canadians and the Chinese in that island.
There seems to be a lot of excitement in the House of Commons and elsewhere in this country about the recently completed wheat and barley deal with the communist administration of mainland China. I should point out to the committee that in my opinion the communist government in Peking has no interest in long term trading with this country, which would be of benefit to both countries, and certainly very little interest in building an understanding between Chinese people and Canadians.
In fact, and there is evidence of this out of the mouths of spokesmen of the government of Peking, they are determined to destroy capitalist countries by military or economic means. The only understanding they wish to achieve is an acceptance by us of the communist philosophy.
Therefore I say that I for one cannot share in the jubilation of those who think that this grain deal, which will bring in a few dollars to this country over the next several years, is a big thing for Canada.
The people of the republic of China in Taiwan-a country which I had the privilege

Supply-Trade and Commerce of visiting recently-are working very hard with relatively few resources to build up their country. As is the case in India, government has a greater role in the economy than in many western countries, but the economy in Taiwan is essentially a free enterprise one.
The rapid growth of population in this country, about 3.5 per cent per year, makes it very difficult to increase per capita consumption of food each year. Only a quarter of this rocky and mountainous island is suitable for farming. Therefore increased food production can be brought about only through the institution of irrigation projects, improving the seeds that are used and fertilizers.
I think hon. members may be interested in hearing something about the recent achievements of the people in this country.
I	shall be brief in this respect. In a few minutes I should like to show that the economy of that island is steadily growing, and it could become an important trading partner of Canada. This is no small country. Some
II	million people live in Taiwan and, as I have said, it is becoming one of the important free enterprise economies in the Pacific area.
I agree with the assistant trade commissioner for Canada in Manila, who writing in the April 22 issue of "Foreign Trade" had this to say:
Many Canadian exporters who have focused their sales efforts on Asia continue to ignore the expanding sales opportunities in Taiwan.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke this morning about the efforts of trade commissioners in the Asian countries, I was sorry that he omitted to refer to this country as an area in which Canadian business could be developed.
In the Asian countries one of the best indications of economic growth is the production of food. Through a co-operative effort on the part of land owners, tenants and agencies of government the Chinese in Taiwan have been so successful in this field that the consumption of food per capita in the rural areas is greater than in any other Asian country.
In 1959 livestock production was four times the level attained in 1946. The volume of production in other farm products was over two and a half times greater in 1959 than in 1946. These increases have been brought about through the land reform program initiated by the present vice president of the republic of China, which program has proceeded through three steps, a reduction of farm rent, the sale of public farm lands and the abolition of the tenancy system.
Since the land reform program was undertaken some 200,000 families who were formerly tenant farmers have become owners of

plots of land. Land owners whose land has been expropriated have been compensated with bonds which are redeemed in rice and sweet potatoes, and stocks in government-owned industries. Thus in a period of 11 years a quiet revolution has taken place in agriculture in that country.
I ask hon. members to compare this with the so-called land reform program on the mainland of China which, as everyone here must know, has been marked by violence, terror, loss of freedom, slave labour and starvation.
Agriculture is the main occupation in Taiwan, but industrial production is growing in food processing, chemicals, machinery, ceramics, textiles and other fields.
A good indication of the growth of industry is the expansion in the use of electric power. In this country eight times as much electricity was used in 1960 as was used in 1955. The great changes which have taken place in this country have occurred because of the hard work and the enthusiasm of the men and women associated with the government, and the response of businessmen, farmers and workers to the leadership which the government has given; and, of course, aid from the United States which has been given at the rate of something like $100 million a year.
I wish to express my admiration for the men and women to whom I have just referred, many of whom I had the privilege of meeting in Taiwan in January of this year. What they are doing for their country is not only of value to the Chinese people in that country but it is also of great value in maintaining the morale of political leaders in southeast Asia who are resisting the influence of the Soviet union and communist China.
In 1960 Canada sold to the Chinese in Taiwan goods of a value of $2,885,642, and imports to Canada from Taiwan came to $1,150,222. The Chinese in that country- and I know this from speaking to many of them-are anxious to increase trade with this country and become less dependent on the United States for machinery, electrical equipment and other things.
Therefore I recommend to the minister that at a very early date the trade commissioner now stationed in Manila should go to Taipei and meet government and business leaders of that country with a view to finding out what Canadians can sell there and informing the Canadian business community of the opportunities that are available.
I wish to advocate the establishment of a Canadian consulate in Taipei as a first step toward bringing about closer business relationships between Canadians and the Chinese of this country. I am sure these improved

relationships would be of commercial benefit to both countries. They would build friendships between Chinese and Canadians which would lead to a greater understanding by the people of this country of the culture and traditions of the Chinese people.
I hope that on the next occasion a minister of the crown makes a trip to the Far East- and I hope that minister will be the Minister of Trade and Commerce-he will be going to celebrate the opening of a Canadian consulate in Taipei, and that he will come back to this house and announce a trade agreement which will be to the benefit both of the people of Taiwan and ourselves. It seems to me this would help to reach the objective of the trade policy described by the minister on April 28 when he said it was to foster the development among trading nations of policies conducive to the development, growth and expansion of mutually beneficial trade.

I regret that on Friday afternoon when the minister made a speech introducing his estimates and submitting them to this committee for approval I was unfortunately absent. I want to assure the hon. gentleman that my absence was not due to lack of interest either in the speech or in the subject matter. It arose merely through some misunderstanding which had arisen the previous day about the business of the house and the impression which had been created that the debate on external affairs would continue on Friday.
However, there is one advantage in not having been here on Friday. I had the opportunity of reading the hon. gentleman's speech and perhaps that gives a better opportunity for analysing it. I shall try in my few remarks today to avoid traversing the ground which was covered in the want of confidence motion moved on Monday of last week and debated on Monday and Tuesday. I regard that debate as one of the most important we have had on the subject of trade for some considerable time. I think that today on the estimates of the department itself it would not be appropriate to repeat the arguments raised then, but if I do not repeat them I do not want to indicate any lack of opinion as to the importance of that discussion in the whole field of foreign trade. It seems to me that that debate did deal directly with the situation as it affects our foreign trade today.
The amendment to the supply motion was, it will be recalled, a motion expressing want of confidence in the government. I might remind the committee of its terms. It read as follows:
That this house regrets the protectionist and inconsistent trade policies of the government and its failure to develop a long term foreign economic policy to enable Canada to participate fully in the
Supply-Trade and Commerce
challenging new opportunities in the field of international trade by implementing a vigorous program to promote the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries and by encouraging the development of an Atlantic economic community.
It seems to me that this amendment came squarely to grips with the issue and that the debate was, as indicated, the best debate on the subject we have had for some considerable time.
My remarks today, to the extent that they are critical, are critical of the government for its failure to place this situation in its proper perspective and its failure to develop long term policies which will be appropriate to meet the challenges that exist today in the field of international trade. The inconsistencies of the government's approach are already beginning to have a very damaging effect and very damaging implications for the future. The speech of the Minister of Finance at Ste. Adele on November 17 of last year, seemed to me to be the kind of speech that is destructive of the development of proper trading relationships with the other trading countries with which we are chiefly concerned. I was critical of it last Tuesday, as appears from the record in Hansard, and I may say I was somewhat amazed that the minister, rather than trying to deal with the criticisms of his speech and of the attitude taken in it, seemed to repeat it and to support it. Indeed, he even added to it. I think that was completely wrong.
It seems to me that the situation confronting Canada today has two or three main aspects. First of all, there is the Sino-Soviet bloc with its trade policies and all their implications for us. The implications of those trade policies are two-pronged. One has to do with upsetting the trade of particular segments of the western trade area, by one process or another, and the other prong, the other danger, lies in its implications to the underdeveloped countries by upsetting their economies. It is an unfortunate fact that a very large number of the underdeveloped countries in the world today possess economies which are largely dependent on the export of one or two basic commodities and that if anything happens in the trading world which leads to a sharp drop in the prices of those particular commodities then the economy of that country is seriously and immediately damaged. As a result of that damage we see a political development, and there is also, of course, an economic set back which makes the country less effective as a potential trading market and trading area. As I view the Russian development, it lies in those two fields.
Anything which can be done to assist these underdeveloped countries to develop their

Supply-Trade and Commerce economies on a wider basis is to our benefit and is to the benefit of the free world as a whole since it enables those countries to develop as free nations, with all the desirable implications contained in that statement, and also to form improved trade relationships with our own country. Thus, on two grounds it is very much in our interest to see these underdeveloped countries improve their conditions and improve them quickly. I have spoken now, about the development of the Russian-Chinese bloc in that sphere of world activity as I see it today.
There is another condition which holds some implications for Canada, a condition which if not handled carefully could be adverse to us. Our agricultural exports would be particularly affected, but it could also affect our exports across the board. I refer to the European trade blocs, the European free trade area and the European common market. These two trade blocs have been discussed a great deal in the house by hon. members on both sides. There seems to be a substantial difference of opinion about the implications attached to the development of the trade blocs.
The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have, in my opinion, a wrong appreciation of this subject and have failed to see what should be done about it. I wish to be sharply critical in this regard. I have read some of the minister's speeches two or three times, because the Minister of Finance, in particular, is always quick to accuse hon. members of misquoting him.
There is no doubt at all that the propositions contained in the speeches of the two ministers relating to that subject have been interpreted as threats of retaliation. Certainly I have interpreted them in this way, and this interpretation is reflected by articles appearing in the newspapers I have read. One article described these speeches as angry little retaliation speeches. Other similar adjectives have been used to describe them. It has been suggested that they contained negative approaches to the problem, and perhaps even destructive approaches.
I do not see how we can appropriately and efficiently develop an economic policy by angry little retaliatory speeches of this kind. These problems arise because of the Sino-Russian bloc and similar organizations in Europe. The implications of those blocs create the atmosphere in which we must develop our trade policy today.
I felt that the Minister of Finance, in seeking to accuse the Leader of the Opposition of dispensing with GATT, did less than justice to my leader's speech. I thought the Leader of the Opposition made a very able

speech and that it was quite unworthy of the Minister of Finance to reply the way he did.
The historical fact is that in 1947, when GATT was developed, the Liberal government of that day played a very important and active part in its development. If one relates the development of GATT to the conditions which existed at the time-at the conclusion of the last war-one will realize that this development was a farsighted arrangement which did much to meet the problems confronting the western world at that time. It provided the machinery through which world trade could be supported and started moving again and, as I have said, the government of that day played a very prominent part, which appears on the record, and speaks well, in my opinion, for that government.
The situation in which we find ourselves today is that the Minister of Finance is attempting to rely on the same machinery, in the form it was at that time, without developing it to meet the new conditions with which we are confronted today. GATT is of course a splendid concept, it embodies a consistent policy, but it is unlikely to fully provide the kind of farsighted development we require today.
In summing up the situation I would say that I felt there was a very apt speech made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres on Monday, April 24. I would like to read his statement as it is recorded at page 3951 of Hansard for April 24, 1961:
On the contrary, in the light of Canada's trade deficits and her increased difficulty in competing in her home markets as well as in foreign markets, because of the disruption of traditional trade relationships, because of the possibility of increased economic competition from the Soviet union and her satellites and because of the paramount necessity of aiding the underdeveloped nations of the world, Canada cannot afford to be without a definite, well-thought-out, long range foreign economic policy. The stakes are too high and the situation too tense for Canada to continue to indulge, as she is now doing, in off the cuff, hit-or-miss trade policies, in apologetic but none the less restrictive trade measures with all her hopes of solving her problems pinned on the loud-talking high pressure salesmanship of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
It seems to me that this statement puts the issues, with which we are confronted in trade fields, very squarely, and perhaps in better language than I could use. This is the type of long term, carefully thought out foreign economic policy that is required today, and that is exactly what we are not now receiving from the minister.
That long term foreign economic policy must be developed on two fronts. The first is the taking of active, positive steps-not just

sitting back watching and criticizing-to better integrate ourselves with Great Britain and ultimately the United States and the two European trade blocs. We must play an active role in integrating these two blocs into a larger Atlantic trade community which will not be restrictive or inward looking, but will be outward looking. This is a step that will require active participation on the part of the government and the minister. We are not receiving this participation now.
Second, proper steps must be taken to assist our secondary industries, which have been dealt cruel blows in the last two years particularly. Those blows have resulted from two or three different causes. First, because of the increased ability of foreign competitors to produce efficiently and cheaply with the resulting natural competition. The second is because our government has not adapted itself to the changed conditions which secondary industry must meet, by assisting secondary industry in meeting the problems, but has, instead, retained certain tax measures that were developed at a time when conditions were completely different, with the result that increased burdens have been placed upon these secondary industries.
There has been no apparent appreciation by the government of these problems. I have been very critical of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for his failure to understand that secondary industry plays a part in our foreign trade policy as well as our domestic trade policy, and that it must be re-established to full, effective participation, because this is a field which provides a great portion of our employment.
I would like to read from the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as reported at page 3945 of Hansard for April 24, 1961 where he was referring to the amendment to the supply motion, moved by the opposition. He is reported as follows:
It purports to speak on the one hand of a free or freer trade area within the Atlantic economic community and in the same breath it expresses regret because, it says, the government has failed to promote the expansion of secondary manufacturing industries in Canada. These two portions are contradictory and represent opposite ends of the economic pole.
They are not inconsistent; they are wholly consistent. One cannot effectively be done without the other. What requires to be done, as well as the things I have spoken about now, international trade, diplomacy, negotiations, and so on, is to take the appropriate steps to rehabilitate secondary industry in the light of today's circumstances.
Incidentally, if you analyse all these things that have happened since 1958 when world exports have gone up by some 16 per cent you will see that our exports have risen by 7 per
Supply-Trade and Commerce cent-I think that is the correct figure-or a little less than half. We are stagnating and losing our relative position. I do not wish to take the minister's individual statistics for two and three months periods, as he did in his speech the other day, and say they are wrong. I do not think they are wrong. Probably they are all correct. I have no quarrel with them, but I do want to point out to him that they must be put in proper perspective and it is this other matter that is really of significance to Canada. His attempt at trying to draw conclusions from trading statistics for two and three months periods is not the appropriate way of dealing with this subject at all. He could take any set of trade figures for any two or three months period and do a great many things with them, depending on what he wants to prove. I do not see that that solves any problem at all, nor is it of any assistance toward setting the country on the right course and, so far as I am concerned, it is important that the country be set on the right course and quickly because we have been losing our trading position and we have been losing our position in maintaining the rate of our development in our own economy internally.
I suppose I could reinforce my argument with quotations. I do not know that that is necessary but there is a particularly good editorial in the April 29 issue of the Financial Post, headed "Pearson's Plea Justifies Study". The editorial quoted part of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition as follows:
The process of Atlantic integration must take place for political as well as for commercial reasons. It is necessary for the prosperity and growth of the Atlantic democracies. But it may soon be necessary also for their survival.
The editorial continues:
Pearson does not advocate any sudden, dramatic or immediate consideration of the Atlantic economies any more than does Prime Minister Macmillan who also believes such an integration is the west's only road to survival. This, like any other international combination, is a very long term proposition and should be regarded as such. President Kennedy has been talking in similar vein.
I could quote the whole editorial which is a particularly good one, but I do not think I should take the time of the committee to do so. There is another sentence that perhaps I should quote. It reads as follows:
If the European trade blocs merge, and all indications suggest they will, and if we on this continent fail to work out a new entente with western Europe, Canada will not for long retain any semblance of independence.
This is the view that the editor who wrote the article took of the importance of this subject. As I say, I could quote at great length. In another article in the same issue of this particular paper they go on and show

Supply-Trade and Commerce how the economy of this country has been stagnating. The editorial is entitled "The Spectre of Stagnation". It reads, in part:
The dollar totals suggest that our recent recessions are only trifling aberrations and that our certain course is progress to a life where everybody makes over $10,000 a year, and where three-car garages are a natural right for every Canadian.
Despite the 1960 recession, GNP-the total value of everything produced, including services and goods-advanced 3 per cent. Personal incomes were up 6 per cent. Consumer spending rose by 4 per cent. This new accounting of how the economy is making out shows GNP is now up fully one third in just five years.
What is important about GNP, however, is not the sometimes stunning dollar totals and their frequently quoted advances.
What matters to practical business planners and to responsible government officials should be real rates of growth. And here the GNP story reveals the spectre of stagnation.
Consider these comfortless figures:
Since 194V, GNP's average annual rate of increase has been almost 8 per cent. This, on the surface, is a remarkable performance. But the average hides the fact that between 1947 and 1956 the annual average was 9 per cent, while in the last four years the rate of increase has been only half as fast-4 per cent per year.
To see how small the real volume gains are, take out the effect of price increases. Then the annual 9 per cent gain from 1947 to 1956 turns into a 5.5 per cent advance and the 4 per cent increase 1956-60 slows to a 1.7 annual rise.
The editorial goes on to develop that theme. In attempting to deal with this subject, in answer to some questions, the minister today did not come up with a long term, well developed statement of policy. I could deal with the answer he gave this morning and puncture many holes in it. He talked about West Indies trade. He did not tell us that we are losing a relative portion of the total there. He did not tell us it was the inconsistent policy of the government of putting one more difficulty in the way that has helped to create more difficulties in this group of islands that are trying to work out a federation which will have full control of these things, a customs union, and so on. He did not tell us he was the very minister who in his other capacity of minister of transport was the one who in one of those short term, quick actions, taken on the spur of the moment, dispensed with the shipping facilities between Canada and the West Indies. He did not tell us that it was that short term policy that did a great deal to damage that trade.
In any event, the point I wish to make is that the minister has been looking at this whole thing under short term, day to day policies, rather than developing a long term policy. Today, in answer to another question, he exhorted management and labour to get together. He spoke about the necessity of management, labour and government getting together to develop productivity. That is very

true, and I am in accord with that statement. Then, he went on to make another typical, enthusiastic speech, exhorting management and labour to do the job. You could hear the speech being repeated so many times. He does this exhortation so well. Indeed, he did it in his football days. He is still at it; without the same characteristic effectiveness.
That exhortation to management and labour is all right. I have no quarrel with it. But he has failed completely to deal with that part requiring to be dealt with which falls under federal jurisdiction, that is what the government can do to assist the economy of the country to assist secondary industry to develop itself. He was completely silent on that subject. He did not give the kind of treatment to that aspect of the matter that would make his exhortations to management and labour effective in that they would know that the third party in this triumvirate was pulling its weight. Instead, we have resentment on the part of management and labour and a feeling that government has failed completely in the area with which it should concern itself.
The government can do and should be doing a great deal. It is the area having to do with the activities of government that should receive the attention of the minister. There should be action on the part of the government, action that so far has not been taken. We have the spectre of the government with its shortsighted policies placing added burdens on productive capacity and on productivity. It has done so in many ways. One way in which it did so was by failing to recognize the need to adapt the taxes that apply to production directly to meet the changed conditions that secondary industries mainly but production industries in general were faced with in the developing world situation. Not only did the government fail to do this but it also in fact increased the burdens that bear directly on production.
The minister did not explain the impact on secondary industries of the added cost brought about by the sharp increase in unemployment insurance charges imposed on both management and labour. One can argue about whether the increase was 35 per cent or what the amount was on each side. It seems to me that, depending on which category is being dealt with, it varied from 20 to 50 per cent. But if you take such an increase in the case of both management and labour, there is an increase in respect of that charge on production alone of somewhere between 40 and 100 per cent.
The minister has not explained at any time since the government took office the impact

of the 50 per cent increase in the old age security tax which was applied directly on production.
Order. I am obliged to interrupt the hon. member to inform him that his time has expired.
Let the hon. member go on.
Will the committee give unanimous consent to the hon. member for Ottawa West continuing?
Agreed.

I want to thank hon. members and I will try not to abuse the privilege unduly. I wish to complete my remarks and I hope they will be of a constructive nature, however destructive of the government they may appear at the moment. The sales tax, which is a direct charge on most production, was increased 10 per cent by the government. The corporation tax has been increased. Other taxes have been increased by way of changes in their application. In the legislation most of these changes appear to be administrative changes and they are somewhat more difficult to describe.
In any event, we must examine immediately the whole field of the applicability of taxation as it applies directly to production with a view to providing the changes and incentives that will enable our productive industries, particularly our secondary industries, to become wholly competitive against imports into this country. That can be done best by making changes in the kind of taxes I have talked about and through the appropriate application of incentives rather than through the minor restrictive tariff measures that the government seems to have applied regularly from time to time since it came into office and which have seemed to do nothing but destroy our trade relations while at the same time rendering no help to those they are intended to help.
The type of tax incentive that has to be applied is a correct use of accelerated depreciation in the proper areas. In the baby budget the government brought forward a measure to provide accelerated depreciation for industries establishing in depressed areas. I have heard the word "phony" used with reference to that measure and while that is not my word it is an apt way to describe it. It is not an atempt to grapple with the problem at all. It does not deal with what is required. It is too restrictive and narrow and the additional allowance on depreciation account for one year is not nearly sufficient. It is simply a useless little measure in terms of what is needed.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
What we need is the use of the weapon of special depreciation on a broad front, first of all in meeting the depressed area problem we have in Canada and then in meeting our export problem. It has to be applied in a carefully planned way. There is quite a reservoir of experience in the application of special depreciation, and I am at a loss to understand why, when the government was dealing with one phase of the matter involving depressed areas, the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not take advantage of governmental experience in using this instrument to bring forward a policy that would be helpful. I suggest to him now that this matter must be examined immediately by the government and a provision for special depreciation brought forward and made applicable in a much wider field and in a wholly different way from what was done in the baby budget. I suggest to him that he will find there is a great deal of experience in the use of such a measure. It was very successful when used in the post-war years in another connection to bring industry into peacetime production. A remarkable job was done on that occasion and I am at a loss to understand why the same kind of job cannot be done now in relation to the problems that confront us today.
Then, of course, there are the problems of straight tax reduction and government waste generally. I think these matters could be more properly discussed either on the finance estimates or on the budget. I do not propose to develop them here other than to suggest that they have a direct applicability to this subject and that care must be used in the kind of policies that are brought forward so that they will not place needless burdens on productivity. I could be very critical of the Minister of Finance and the unemployment insurance fund so far as investments and so on are concerned. These matters must be examined. They are not only a responsibility of the Minister of Finance but, because of their implication, of the whole ministry and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in particular.
Then there are adaptations of the sales tax. There are certain aspects of the applicability of the sales tax that must be examined again in the light of the problems confronting us today. It is a somewhat difficult tax to speak about because one has to deal with so many regulations and its applicability is not an easy thing to define in a few sentences. I am suggesting that it must be examined in relation to its applicability to all aspects of production. It is not just good enough to say that it does not apply to certain manufacturers and so on. A whole detailed examination is required.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Then we have all the other taxes and their applicability. There is this whole problem of the development of the very latest and best facilities that are available for secondary industry and for productive capacity. We must examine this field at once in order to see what measures-mainly tax measures-we can take in order to see to it that instead of plants engaged in production for export and for use in Canada being obliged to carry on with what I can call roughly now, for the purpose of this point, second rate production machinery or machinery that is not quite the latest and best for its purpose, we must make it economically possible for them to replace that machinery and equipment with the very best that is available in the world. We must examine our tax applicable to that problem with a view to providing the incentive that would enable industry to take the steps I am sure we all desire them to take.
Then there is the question of our general corporation tax which is very high. When we are talking about a corporation tax rate of 50 per cent or 49 and three it will be seen that we have placed a very heavy direct burden on these corporations. If they are to provide the jobs required, we must examine this tax structure in order to see that we are not placing on them a burden that negates the development of their productive capacity for the production of goods and the provision of the jobs that our economy requires.
As to the rate of taxes, it is extremely hard to make a comparison. I for one have not been able to get in a precise way the comparable figures for other western trading nations because the taxes are not exactly comparable. For that reason I have avoided using specific rates. However, in trying to check into this subject I get the impression that in the great western trading nations there is probably no other country in which the implication of taxation in this field is so heavy. As I say, that is not something that I can support with precise statistics because I just have not been able to get them in a form in which I thought it was fair to put them forward having regard to the slightly different applicability. But as I tried to find out about taxation and the German production, the Netherlands production and British production I formed the impression, at least in my own mind, that ours is much heavier in its implication and that, if we are to enable our secondary industry and our other production industry to compete successfully, we must make the adjustments necessary to meet that situation.
The committee has been very kind to me in allowing me to complete these remarks about this aspect of the matter. I feel very strongly that this aspect of the matter must
[Mr. Mcllraith.l

be dealt with as part of our plan, that it is useless to talk about trade in today's circumstances without talking about that aspect of it as well as the other matter of duties and volume of merchandise exports and imports.
I hold the view that the kind of thinking that is required now is bold and imaginative thinking if we are to retain our position among the foremost trading nations of the world. As far as I am concerned nothing less will do. To me it is shocking that we have the extent of unemployment we have in this country. To me there are direct reasons for it. I know that there is some easing of the situation in the United States but to me a great part of it exists by reason of policies within our own country that we could control. I am not content to have that condition exist and to have the short term, hit-or-miss policies that the present government has applied to trade. It seems to me that any narrow, isolationist or increasingly protectionist policy is completely out of step with history or developments today in the world.
I have been sharp in my criticism of the present government under the present Prime Minister for adopting confusing and contradictory trade policies. I have made that matter clear every session. I could recount the starting from 1957. There was Mont Trem-blant and the 15 per cent trade diversion speeches. They are just a series of shortsighted contradictory little statements. That thing is taking this country into a period of economic stagnation. We are receding in our world position in trade and there is no need for it. As the minister correctly said this morning, our industrial management and our Canadian people have the capacity for something much better than that. The government must provide the atmosphere in which they can do what they have the capacity to do.
We debated another subject here for some eight days this year and it seemed to me that none of the lessons of this country in the first half of the 1930's were learned by the present government.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member interjects but I can recall to him that I am perhaps one of the few members here who saw the government of that day in operation. I am not going to go back and traverse that ground again but I could not help but think in the customs tariff legislation the concept of trade of the present government had too much of the concept of trade of the government of that day and trade policies which were proved to be wrong and which history and our own experience repudiate. That government brought us into a blind alley. I hope this government will not do that. I want to

make my remarks today a warning to the government and a request that they look at these things and examine them closely.
In those days the unemployment figures were not mere statistics to most of the older members although they may be that to some of the very young. However, to most of the older ones they are not that. They represented very real suffering in that era. They are shockingly high in this era again. It is true that we have social security that prevents the hardships from showing up and becoming apparent as they were in those days. Nevertheless, the problem is there just the same. The destructive value to individual human life is there just the same and we must deal with it. We must not allow blundering policies of this kind to be carried on through default in our criticism here to impel the government to change. We must bring forward these criticisms, as I see it, in order to impel the government to examine the problems and to make changes. We must, of course, try to be constructive in doing it.
The ways in which we can be constructive in it are, as I say, among many others by the government developing a carefully thought out, long term foreign economic policy for this country; by the government taking positive steps at the ministerial level to build up a good working relationship with the trading countries of western Europe which are in the two European trading blocs, with a view to bringing those countries in a larger and better relationship with the whole Atlantic community, in which we will take our full and active part. This will involve the United States, of course, and many of the other related countries.
When that is done, we must see that this long term objective keeps that Atlantic trading area an outward looking area, because if it succeeds in that it will solve this problem about which I spoke very briefly. I refer to the problem of the underdeveloped countries. It will provide the kind of trading area in which those underdeveloped countries can get stable markets for their commodities. It will remove that fluctuation of price of their commodities which is so destructive of them. It will do more to assist those underdeveloped countries than these very good, but direct contributions which the western world makes to them.
It seems to me that this kind of policy would be more helpful to these underdeveloped countries than the direct contributions which they are receiving. This direct aid is necessary, and I am not criticizing it; but it is this kind of positive policy that will meet this problem.
It is this kind of policy that will again bring us back into a position and keep us
Supply-Trade and Commerce in the forefront of the world as a country offering the best opportunities for our young people who are born here, and for young people of other countries who wish to come here to join with us in the development of the best possible life for individual human beings.

Mr. Chairman, I think the compliments one usually gives to the minister can be largely by-passed at this time. I should like to say that I have noticed one difference in the Department of Transport since the Minister of Trade and Commerce left that department. When he was minister it used to be that you could get a reply to a letter in two or three days. It now takes anywhere from two to three weeks for the department to reply to a letter. However, we are not dealing with the estimates of the Department of Transport and I will leave this matter until a later time.
The minister's remarks were almost nonexistent on the small business branch and its operations. When one looks at the number of people employed in the small business branch, when one tries to find out what its budget is, and when one reads the rather obscure outline in the minister's annual report of what the small business branch is trying to do, one begins to question very much certain promises of this government.
I think all hon. members of this committee, whatever their party, have been intrigued by the statements of the Prime Minister that the Kennedy administration in the United States has really looked to Canada for its example; or if not that, if a more restricted explanation is given, Canada-the Conservative party-has been in the forefront in measures to meet our present economic difficulties and the United States are following along behind. This is almost ridiculous when one looks at this particular aspect of the government's promises and its field of operation, and I refer to the small business section.
The Minister of Finance gave us an indication the other day of just how relatively small a response or opening there has been as a result of the small business loan legislation enacted this session. Certainly in the first month and a half of operation there was a most discouraging rate of interest in this legislation.
Then we look at what the small business branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce is doing. I do not know, but the minister could probably tell us just how much the branch costs. I see that they had fewer employees last year than they had two years ago. We have seen little indication that the

Supply-Trade and Commerce branch has done anything other than publish these two pamphlets, which have their value but are not unduly exciting. I refer to the "Small Business" manual and "Selling to the Canadian Government".
In the annual report some claims are made, in connection with the small business branch, to the effect that it is handling a great many inquiries; that it is becoming a clearing house for business inquiries. As a former librarian who kept statistics on the number of people who came into a library and the questions they asked, I know that statistics are not going to necessarily reveal a true pattern of what the branch is doing. However, I think the minister should tell us just what these six people handled in 1960, in terms of inquiries. What kind of inquiries were they, and how much effort went into replying to them? I should like to know how much duplication there may be in what is being done by the small business branch and by other government branches in terms of providing information. I can put it most bluntly by saying this to the minister. You have a branch here with six employees, and the branch is set up to handle business inquiries from the whole of Canada. This is nonsensical. Is the minister going to tell us, or would he argue that six people can answer the business inquiries that may properly be raised by small businessmen throughout the country?
What about your party?

I am quite prepared to acknowledge that perhaps these six men are handling it at the present time, but the only reason they are doing so is because the country does not know anything about the branch and the functions it is carrying out. I have yet to meet a small businessman who has really heard about this branch and the role it is playing. What liaison does it really have with the people?
The report says this branch has been working with associations, and so on; but what can six people do? We had this big hullabaloo from the minister and his department in relation to the foreign trade drive. This is excellent, I believe. I think most of us believe it has filled a role. However, when one goes through the estimates and looks at the tremendous sums required to keep offices going in Beirut, Belfast, Berne, Bogota, Bombay, Bonn, Boston, Buenos Aires, and so on, and then one looks at this little pittance here of six people working in an area where the Conservative party made a great many promises when it was not a government, when it was seeking election, one cannot help but be struck by certain paradoxes.
The minister has never really dealt with this matter. What is this government doing through this branch? Why bother to set up something as petty as this? I think we deserve some explanation in this connection. While he is at it, the minister might tell us, since according to his report this small business branch did provide the background information for the Small Business Loans Act, why loans under the act seem to be moving so slowly. Why is it that I hear complaints from small businessmen to the effect that, really, the act has not opened up much for them at all.
The next matter upon which I should like to touch relates to the census and the whole question, not so much of the operation of it but the controversial part of it.
I do not think any member of this committee need be ashamed of being a Canadian nationalist. I happen to be one, and as a Canadian nationalist I am still very much bothered about the census arrangements and about the changes that took place. I could agree with the changes and I would not quibble about the cost of them in so far as it suited one element of the population which believed it was entitled to, or needed, certain kinds of information. But I put it to the minister this way. When the census enumerator comes around I am going to tell the census enumerator, whether it is question No. 10 or the next question, that I am a Canadian and that this nonsense of ethnic origins in terms of so many of the people of this country does not mean a thing.
I hope the minister has read an article by Mr. McGeachy called "Goats, bathtubs and Christmas trees-they're all in the census". He makes one point in connection with question No. 10 which I think is important. He is talking about the census inquiry regarding ethnic origin and he says:
For some citizens this is a realm of sheer conjecture or family legend. But even correct answers don't, as a rule, mean a thing. For instance, Mr. Diefenbaker will no doubt have to answer "German" to the question (so would Queen Elizabeth if she lived here) but is there anything noticeably Germanic about the P.M.? Does he still belong to a Germanic "cultural group"? He's rather a solemn man; but this trait may well come from his maternal Scottish ancestry.
Mr. McGeachy is having a bit of fun, but it is still a very important consideration and I should like to put this question to the minister. When are we going to have a chance in this country to be Canadians and to forget about this ethnic nonsense? I should like to read to the minister a poem which appeared on this subject in the Fort William Times Journal. I think that in terms of metre it might be better than one usually finds in

newspaper columns. It is by a writer called Lloyd W. Zapfe and the title is "Reveille". It goes:
"Breathes there a man", the poet said and questioned if his soul were dead enough, to care not to extol, the virtues of his "Better Ole".
But what of this fair land of snow? where self-made men may come and go unfettered; paradoxically Canadians they cannot be!
Dieppe and Vimy knew them well;
The North Atlantic's cold grey hell and Europe's skies, they took in stride.
Yet they must show not native pride.
Five generations count for nought;
The Redman scarce deserves a plot, for stranger is he not? Forsooth!
He but arrived with Sabre tooth!
Now Nordic, Latin, Slav, take heart, perchance someday you may be part of this great land; so justly famed:
A first class citizen; acclaimed!
Countdown.
Damn the politician's crust!
Let's shoulder ballots if we must and storm this Fortress Ennui; raise up our colors. All to see our native land attenuated, our citizens un-hyphenated.
This particular attitude is one which I share completely. I do not want to overstate the issue. As a political issue it certainly should not be approached on partisan lines. But I should like to ask the minister again: when, in Canada, are we going to be able to declare ourselves Canadians and not in terms of citizenship? I think this is a matter about which the hon. gentleman should come out into the open. We grant the compromise which has been made. We are not critical of the compromise if a certain group in French Canada wants certain kinds of information, but I fail to see why the fact that they want this information about their ethnic group should mean taking away from a large number of the rest of us the right to identify ourselves as Canadians. Good Lord, I have not the vaguest idea of the ethnic group to which I belong, but, if we are to go far enough back into the past, Mr. McGeachy has shown that the Prime Minister and the Queen are wonderful examples of the ridiculous side of this whole question.
It seems to me that the basis of approach to a matter such as this has always been compromise. I should like to suggest to the minister that there are a tremendous number of people in English Canada who are ready to see an end of compromise in this situation. I would also like to suggest to him that if the area I represent is any criterion there is building up a very strong sentiment against the negative aspect of the census. I say it is a negative aspect when after five and six
Supply-Trade and Commerce generations you are still searching through your father's line to find out what your ethnic origin might be.
One other aspect of the census has already been touched on a number of times in the house. The shorter hon. member for Halifax gave us a statement reported at page 4012 of Hansard concerning the qualifications of the census commissioners. We were all amused when he said:
Each of these commissioners met the following qualifications: a good education with subsequent professional or business experience in a supervisory capacity-
Then the hon. member for Trinity interjected:
Good loyal Conservatives.
After which the hon. parliamentary secretary went on:
-intimate knowledge of the census district; proven executive and organizing ability; tact, good judgment and ability to deal with the public. The salary is $1,200.
I have brought this point to the attention of the minister before. There are smart Conservatives and there are dull Conservatives and there are stupid Conservatives. There are needy Conservatives, there are some in moderate circumstances and there are some who are affluent. Without going into the situation that all the census commissioners in the constituencies of Port Arthur and Fort William are, to my personal knowledge, good Conservatives, some of whom did attend the Conservative party rally here, I am wondering, in relation to the commissioners selected, whether they really did fill the bill in terms of being smart, or being needy, or being competent.
I am not going to single out names but I have certainly very serious doubts as to whether some of the census commissioners at the lakehead possess these qualifications and I would just like to say to the minister that if he is going to appoint Conservatives, if he sets up an organization in co-operation with Mr. Grosart using the services of his parliamentary secretary to make the arrangements across Canada, if he has a census organization based upon the Conservative party, why does he not accept a certain responsibility for seeing that he gets good and smart Conservatives for the job? I am willing to accept that there are good Conservatives and smart Conservatives. But if you want to search at the lakehead you will find Conservatives who have more ability than the ones who were picked, and Conservatives who are in greater need. I suggest to the minister that not only in his role as a minister of the crown but as an important figure in the party he has a direct responsibility in this regard.
