Supply-Trade and Commerce You might say, Mr. Chairman, that to talk about Conservative party organization on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce is out of order. I insist that the minister himself and his parliamentary secretary have made it an integral part of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I was expecting that. I think the members of our party expected that. We are experienced enough to know that as long as we have this government in power we are going to have this pragmatic approach. I come back once again to the point I have made. There are smart Conservatives and there are dull Conservatives. There are affluent ones and there are needy ones. Why the tendency seems to be to give these jobs always to the affluent and to the dull is a little beyond my comprehension. I suggest this may reflect weakness in the Conservative party organization, and, with an election coming up, this might well prove very dangerous for the party. I think that when we come to the relevant part of the estimates the minister might take us into his confidence and tell us just how these people were picked. I know it has been easy in most of the constituencies because there are 207 representatives of the Conservative party here and their liaison with the shorter member for Halifax has been close. I have noticed the interchange of communication and the change in reputation of the smaller hon. member for Halifax as a result of this important role. I am thinking more of the constituencies not represented by Conservatives; the unfortunate places. I would like the minister to tell us where he received the advice as to the appointments. I am not suggesting that he should have come to me, or the hon. member for Fort William. I would not like to accept the responsibility of passing judgment on the dullness or smartness of Conservatives. However, I think it might have been better if he had turned to the national employment service for this information.
I also wonder if the minister has talked this over with the Minister of Labour. The minister may find that by by-passing the national employment service he has done an injustice to one of his colleagues. I have had many inquiries from individuals who would like these census jobs, particularly students.
I always advise them to telephone Art Shewchuk, the president of the Port Arthur Conservatives constituency association. I would like to ask the minister if I am giving them the right advice. I was dealing earlier with the small business branch. Everyone likes to run an efficient operation and I want to make sure I am sending these individuals to the right horse's mouth.
[Mr. Fisher.l

I do not intend to say anything further about this but I do hope the minister can tell us more about the matter. Where should these people who are scrambling for jobs go? I think the smaller member for Halifax told the house that these individuals should apply to the census commissioners themselves but I have a hunch that they need clearance from the local constituency association, and that is why I have been sending them there. If I have been committing an error I would like to know so that I may correct it. I hope the minister will straighten out this situation for me.
The last point I wish to touch upon in connection with the minister's department relates to information about the expenditures of this department. I would suggest that one really does not get as much information from appendix F in the annual report as one might like regarding the operations of this department. Since the public accounts are always somewhat in arrears so far as presenting a pattern, and since the estimates give a very incomplete picture of the costs involved in operating the various aspects of the department, I wonder whether it might be possible for the minister to expand on that information. Perhaps I could make this clear to him by pointing out to him that under heading no. 2 "Expenditures by Main Item Only" there appear some very large figures. However, when one turns to statement No. 1, expenditures for fiscal years, where one is supposed to find the details, there is not a very adequate breakdown. If an attempt is made to understand the very complex role carried out by the standards branch, and there are a number of functions that branch performs which may be complementary but are quite distinct, one cannot really ferret out this information. I pointed out the small business branch earlier as another example which, as the minister will remember, started its first year of operation with $35,000. I do not know whether that total amount has been spent, and I would like to know how much the operation of that branch costs, and what plans there are for the expansion of its expenditures. I would like to know how much of this money is represented by salaries to staff, and how much is represented by the cost of reference work.
In conclusion I would like to say that the minister's speech in regard to the whole question of trade, which he made at the lakehead about a month ago, received good response from the businessmen there. Those businessmen accepted the remarks he made because they felt the minister intended to do something about trade policy. I have on a number of occasions since heard criticisms, and have witnessed a change in attitude, which now

seems to be that the minister has a lot of pep and enthusiasm; however, what is the government doing in a practical or concrete way to carry forward this enthusiasm and exhortations to do better?
The minister came into that area of Ontario where we live and made some challenging and enthusiastic statements but I do not think he can leave the situation at that. We would like to see some follow through in this regard. When are his officials going to arrive in that area to follow up that pep rally the minister attended? The hon. member for Ottawa West in fact asked the same questions although he cast them in a more general but complicated manner relating to the department's trade policy as a whole. I would like to ask the minister now how he is going to follow up this picture of his so that something is filled in around the general hosannas and florets?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to answer some of the questions put to me by the hon. member for Port Arthur. First of all he asked about the total outlay of the small business branch. The total amount is $70,000. The allocation of that $70,000 is, to staff $65,500, but the actual expenditure there at the present time is about half that. There are six individuals working in that branch and the total allocation is for 13.
The hon. member asked if I could tell him something about the activities of the small business branch itself, and I will now try to do so. The small business branch serves as a focal point for the small businessman to come to discuss his problems and to receive assistance and advice. The present rapidly changing economic conditions often pose particular problems for small businessmen. The branch was established in order that it might provide a specialized service to help small businessmen in dealing with these problems. The small businessman receives assistance and advice from the branch on such matters as the establishment of a business enterprise, capital and other financial requirements, unfair business practices, government procurement, government services generally, accounting, and other fields of business management. The branch actively studies the problems of small business and, in co-operation with other departments, advises the government on possible courses of action to alleviate such difficulties.
The branch serves as a clearing house for small businessmen, in that, if it cannot provide information from its own resources, it directs the businessman's inquiries to the appropriate government departments and agencies which have the required specialized knowledge. The branch can also provide
Supply-Trade and Commerce businessmen with information on federal government procurement and, in this connection, has published a manual entitled "Selling to the Canadian Government". The business community has requested more than 10,000 copies of this document. In co-operation with manufacturers' associations, the branch prepares other types of business publications aimed at assisting small business.
I would be very interested if hon. members would tell me of any small or large businessman who has made inquiries of this branch but has not received satisfactory information or service. We in the Department of Trade and Commerce pride ourselves in doing everything that is humanly possible to give the service and information that is asked for. We may not give all that is asked or perhaps even satisfactory information, but we attempt to do so. If we do not, then we want to kno why. I would appreciate hearing information in detail from any hon. member regarding any incident as to how we have let any small businessman down in regard to information which he has asked for but has not received.
The hon. member also asked for information regarding the small loans program. I have just been handed some information in this respect. From January 19, to March 31, 1961, there were 334 loans to a value of $2,034,628. The average size of such loans was about $6,000. This emphasizes the small loan feature.
The director advises me that loan activity is expanding very rapidly. For instance, in March the loans were about three times the number of those in February, and expansion is expected to continue at a similar rapid rate. He explains that, after all, it takes some time to get these operations going, but activity is stepping up all the time.
The next thing the hon. member asked about was the census itself. He emphasized the desirability of a Canadian being able to say that he or she is a Canadian. This is one of the prime purposes of the revised census form. If the hon. member will look at question No. 9 he will see that it reads as follows:
Country of citizenship.
Are you a Canadian?
I do not know of any better way that a Canadian citizen can say that he is a Canadian than by being asked "Are you a Canadian?" and answering "Yes". If there is any better way of saying it, I should like to be advised of it by the hon. member.
The hon. member then said he regretted that ethnic origins are asked for. I wish to advise him that there are some 18 million-odd people in Canada and a very large proportion of those find it very important to

Supply-Trade and Commerce know the ethnic origin of the people of Canada. That is the reason why the question is asked.
The hon. member asked if I could tell him how a Canadian citizen goes about becoming an enumerator for the coming census. The simple answer is that he applies to the census commissioner in his area. They are the ones who will decide who will be the census enumerator.
The minister should see how it was done in Vancouver East.

The hon. member asked if we could expand the details given in appendix F in the annual report. I am glad to be able to say that we shall be happy to look into the possibilities of doing that. We want to give all the information possible without having the document too unwieldly, and we shall do everything possible to give more information in that appendix.
The last question asked by the hon. member was what follow-up is my department giving to what he described as the pep talks that I am giving around the country. After listening to the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Ottawa West I seem to get the impression that they think there is something bad and distasteful about being enthusiastic and trying to enthuse other people into a greater selling effort and a greater producing effort. That is what I have been trying to do across this country since I took over as minister. I have been trying to point out what the citizens of this country must do in order to help themselves. This is what I have been trying to point out and I will be doing this further at trade conferences which are being conducted in various provinces across this country at the invitation of provincial governments, chambers of commerce, and so on. I shall be indicating to the businessmen who are attending those conferences, and who have already attended them in very large numbers, exactly what services this government department has at the beck and call of businessmen who are interested in going into the export market, and to try to induce more to go into the export market, telling them how we can help them.
At least half of those conferences are going to be devoted to the problems faced by individual businessmen in the domestic commerce of this country; in other words, trying to sell their goods and services here in Canada.
I spoke in the hon. member's home town of Port Arthur a few weeks ago. He was present at the meeting. Evidently he thought of my speech as a pep talk and nothing more. Some of the businessmen who attended thought it was useful. He asked me what our

department is going to do to follow up, and when my officials are going to go up there again. I can assure him that I have not enough officials in this department to go often to every city in Canada, much as we would like to do so. We operate what we think is an efficient department here in Ottawa. Our doors are always open. We try to give them all the information possible. I have tried to do so in my speeches to businessmen generally across Canada and to anybody else who would like to come here and talk to us. I have tried to tell them that we have a tremendous number of services available to businessmen right here in Ottawa. We cannot go to every city; we cannot talk to all of the businessmen in their places of business, but we have services available to them here, and if they have not the desire and the initiative, when they have problems, to ask us about them, to write to us or to come here and talk to us, then I am afraid that is their own concern.
But a great many businessmen have that kind of interest. A tremendous number come to us every day in the week and we try to give them all the services that we possibly can to help them do their job better, to make sales, to make jobs available to Canadians. If the hon. member, or any other hon. member, knows of any businessmen who have come here and found that we did not give them service, that our services were not available to them, that we were not as helpful as we should have been, I would honestly appreciate it if he would give us the information or let me know because I want to check up on those particular branches which are not giving the service. I know that all of my staff are equally interested to hear of any information of that kind. We pride ourselves on trying to do a good job. We intend to keep on trying to do it and any help the hon. member or any other hon. member can give us in assisting us in this regard will be most appreciated. I think I have answered the hon. member's questions.

I have a couple of questions. First of all, on the citizenship matter, the minister says that the census form allows one to state very clearly that he is a Canadian, but under what framework? This is my quarrel with the form. Question No. 9 under "country of citizenship", asks "Are you a Canadian? If not of what country are you a national or a citizen?" I do not see how one can look at this question without turning to question No. 10 which reads:
To what ethnic or cultural group did you or your ancestor (on the male side) belong on coming to this continent?

I am just suggesting to the minister that one question demeans from the other, and the necessity of a question such as "Are you a Canadian" under the label "Country of citizenship" to me is unnecessary.
The comments by the minister in part of his rather fighting-back attitude were along the lines of asking did I know of any examples of people who had a poor response from the small business branch. I do not. That was the point of my argument. My point was, if you have a branch of six members dealing with problems of the whole country there must be a certain inadequacy in the kind of service they perform. If businessmen across the country are responding and asking questions, how can six men do the job? I am just suggesting to the minister that there is a certain irony in the fact that we spend $52,000 in Beirut and $65,000 in Berne, and so on, and yet in this very important aspect of our work the minister has six members in Ottawa.

Perhaps I can answer that. We could enlarge the number of people employed in that branch up to double the number and more than that any time we wish to, as soon as the pressure of business justifies it. That branch is there. As far as I know it is well known to businessmen across the country. When I go to speak in the various provinces in the weeks ahead I am going to re-emphasize the fact that the small business branch is available to give service. We want as many small businessmen in Canada as possibly can to come to us, write to us, and ask us questions. There is nothing I would sooner do than quadruple this staff and I will do so as soon as the pressure of inquiries from small businessmen asking for information justifies it. I am not going to enlarge the branch just for the sake of enlarging it. I will do so as soon as there is any justification for doing so. I would love to see the branch consist of 50 people working full time. That would make me very happy because it would show that we were able to give small businesses a great deal of help of the kind they need to enable them to do more business and employ more Canadians. If the hon. member can act as a salesman for us in any way by telling people what we have available and if all other hon. members will do likewise, I will welcome it very sincerely indeed.
With regard to the census questions, I am afraid I cannot explain that matter any better than I have. The question is asked, "Are you a Canadian", and you say "Yes". If that does not give you a chance to say you are a Canadian, I do not know what does. I cannot think of how you can put it any more clearly. The next question has nothing 90205-6-272
Supply-Trade and Commerce to do with being a Canadian citizen because it asks, "What ethnic group did you belong to before you came to our shores?" You cannot be a Canadian citizen before you come to the shores of this country. These are two completely different questions. They were thought out carefully and I hope they are satisfactory to the Canadian people. I do not know how we can make them any more satisfactory.

As to the last rebuttal of the minister with relation to his appearance at Port Arthur, I think he misunderstood me. He said that he went to the lakehead and made his speech and he thought there was an enthusiasm that I apparently did not see. The minister is mistaken. I was glad he came to the lakehead and made his speech, and there is nothing wrong with putting on a pep rally. It was especially fortunate that it came at the time it did because, as the minister knows from the remarks he heard there, our area has suffered very severely from unemployment this winter. I give the minister credit for raising the spirits of the people who were at the meeting. I was simply suggesting to him that there needs to be a following up and building up of the kind of liaison that the minister is establishing in a very popular way. If I can do anything to advertise any of the services of his department, I will be only too glad to do so.
The last remark I would make is that there comes a point of diminishing returns in generating enthusiasm. All the generation of enthusiasm in the world will begin to taper off and the fillip will go out of it unless there is some concrete success in relation to it. Whether the minister is a success as Minister of Trade and Commerce we have no clue yet. I think there are indications that we are going to have to wait a bit longer to find out, and I would simply suggest to the minister that we will not know the measure of his success or the measure of the success of his rallying enthusiasm until we see some changes and developments both in regard to external trade and in helping small businesses. I do not think I can put it any more fairly than that.

I do not want to carry on this debate interminably but I do want to point out that in the speeches I have made since I became minister I have tried not to be simply a pep rally leader or somebody going throughout the country in that way, and I tried to point that out this morning in my opening remarks. I took it that some hon. members who heard me speak in the house on Friday got the idea that I thought everything was fine, that all we had to do was to

Supply-Trade and Commerce carry on doing what we are doing and everything would work out for the best. I said that I wanted to correct that right away and I did.
I have tried to point out that all across the world, as I said once again this morning, we face the toughest competitive situation this country has faced since before the last war. It is a very serious competitive situation because countries that were formerly our markets are now our toughest competitors. I have tried to outline what the government is willing to do, can do and is doing to help business. I have tried to point out what management and labour must do in co-operation with the government, that this is a three-way operation involving government, management and labour and that we all have a big job. Nobody can turn to the other fellow and say, "It is your job; it is not mine".
That is what the Minister of Labour has done.

It is a job for the 18 million people in the country. I have not tried to make out that all you have to do is to hold pep rallies and everything will be fine. I have tried to point out that we are up against a very tough situation. I have tried to point out what has to be done and to urge people to do it. I hope they will do it. If they do, if we can work together in the way of the peoples of Europe and Japan did in pulling themselves up out of the slough of the war to the top of the heap in 15 years, then we, like them can have full employment. We can have our very high standard of living, the highest in the world, I believe. But I say again that it is up to us and that people cannot simply sit back and wait for some miracle that the government is going to create. Nobody is going to create any miracles.
Let the government give some leadership.

We all have a job to do. The sooner we recognize it, the sooner we are going to get under way and the sooner we will be at the top of the heap where the countries of Europe now find themselves as a result of such efforts.
Why does the government not give leadership?
That is exactly what the government is doing.

Mr. Chairman, I think the Department of Trade and Commerce is probably one of the most important departments for


settling, not temporarily but permanently, the unemployment problem, provided the department is properly run in relation to Canada's needs.
Let me say at the outset that I think the minister has made a worthy effort; he has tried to inject some life into Canada's business and industrial community. However, I think his effort has not been enough, has not produced what we had a right to expect from the Minister of Trade and Commerce because in my view, the main cause of unemployment is the lack of outside markets in which to sell our surplus production.
We need new markets. We are told at one point that our exports have gone up, and a month later we are told that they have dropped. Perhaps it is true, but one sure thing is that Canada, with a population of 18 million, produces much more than it can consume. We must find markets outside Canada, throughout the world, for this surplus production.
Has there been a real effort made in that direction up to now? We know we are selling abroad. Just recently, we sold some wheat. That is fine, and we welcome it. However if you take a closer look at the statistics, you find that 40 per cent of our exports are agricultural products, approximately 40 per cent are raw materials, and only 20 per cent are manufactured or semi-manufactured products. When we sell raw materials abroad rather than manufactured or partly manufactured products, this works to the benefit of the workers in other countries and to the detriment of our own workers.
I was reading recently in the Financial Time for March 17, 1961 an article written by Mr. Rae, vice president and general manager of the North American Division of Atlas Steels Limited. Here is what he had to say on the particular point I was just making:
(Text):
The only effective solution to Canada's small market for most of our industries is active development of markets outside Canada.
(Translation):
That, in my view, is what the Department of Trade and Commerce should do: it should tackle this task earnestly so as to find new markets; otherwise, we can expect steady unemployment for years to come, and I do not think the Canadian people, no matter how good-natured they are, will be prepared to put up with such a situation much longer.
There are those who claim that to get a better share of the foreign market, we would have to step up production, as this would probably lower the cost of our goods. How

can we step up production when we already have surpluses that cannot be sold? It does not make sense. We must find new markets, and reliable markets.
Here is another quotation from the same article:
(Text):	,
Because we make products used almost entirely by industry, not directly by consumers, our major export markets are the world's industrial areas such as the United States, United Kingdom and Europe.
(Translation):
This means that we are losing here the jobs we should be giving to our workers. There are plenty of markets, of course, but our prices are perhaps too high and that is a bad thing.
Indeed, the minister himself pointed this out, because the same writer said:
(Text):
On February 7th, here in Toronto, our minister of trade and commerce said it was necessary for industry to reduce its costs to be competitive overseas.
(Translation):
That is something we admit. But how can we manage to cut down the cost of our products? There might be a way, if some emergency forced us to use it, and that would be to establish some sort of controlled economy which would settle everything. But this does not seem quite in order in a democracy such as we conceive it. However, the government could, as did certain other governments, provide grants to enable our prices to meet those of other goods on the foreign market at least for the first year. This policy would enable those industries to decrease costs by increasing their production so that, after a year, or perhaps two or three, Canadian manufacturers could sell their goods on the foreign markets at a competitive price.
Has this been done? I do not think so. I hold that this is one of the first points the present minister should watch.
As a matter of fact, in his Toronto statement the author finds that our attitude is contradictory, and he says:
(Text):
Two weeks later he was reported to have said increases in taxes were inevitable in 1961. I find it impossible to justify these two statements or to believe he does not consider taxes are a cost item.
(Translation):
And this is true, as the member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) pointed out earlier. Therefore, the entire department should look carefully into our whole taxation system, because something must be done.

Canada cannot wait any longer. Even though the minister did all he could, if it is not enough, he should seek counsel from the other ministers to determine what are Canada's needs at this time, because, let us not forget it, unless we find some way of disposing of our surplus production, no matter what government is in power in a few years from now, because of the present emergency we shall have to resort to a controlled economy. I do not believe that Canadians are too anxious to see that happen. We had to do it during the war because that was an emergency; we controlled prices and production costs; we controlled everything, in order to maintain a war-time economy. That can be done in cases of emergency, and if the situation remains as it is today-as reflected by the serious unemployment-and if the government fails to increase our markets, we shall be compelled to implement a trading policy which, as I said earlier, is not considered appropriate for Canada.
In the same article, Mr. Rae had this to say also on the subject:
(Text):
In order to manufacture our products at prices that will enable us to meet competition from imports we have to have modern, high-volume, efficient equipment. In order to justify purchasing such equipment, we have to have markets much larger than Canada alone provides.
(Translation):
And that is a fact. The whole question revolves around the matter of finding ways of disposing of our surplus production.
Mr. Chairman, we find ourselves in the midst of a situation that did not exist 10, 15 or 20 years ago. We see the idea of a common market gaining ground in Europe and involving in certain parts a free trade area. This will necessarily affect Canada's foreign trade.
Now what is the government doing in the face of such a situation?
We were approached by the British at Mont Tremblant. We were invited to consider the matter of free trade among the British nations. Did the government at least take the trouble to study the suggestion, to determine whether there was anything in it that might improve our situation? I do not blame the government for not accepting it immediately, but I do blame the government for failing to give it serious consideration, for failing to set up a committee of qualified people to study the matter, so that we might have known definitely whether it was possible for Canada to join a free trade area.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
We are now witnessing the development of the common market. And I will say this, Mr. Chairman. The Conservative party, which had always been considered as more empire-minded than any other party, will probably be responsible for breaking the commonwealth ties, in view of its stubborn refusal to recognize the situation facing the U.K. at the present time.
Faced with the common market, the United Kingdom has to keep in step. Last week, the United Kingdom indicated that it would necessarily join the common market, but before doing so, would have to consult with the commonwealth countries in view of the preferential tariff prevailing between those countries. Therefore, Canada will have to follow the suggestions which have been made both to the minister (Mr. Hees) and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and try not only to develop a common market area with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries, but try to develop a common market within the 15 NATO countries. Instead of trying, through increased tariffs- whether disguised or not-to protect a dwindling industry, the government should try to widen its perspective and find a means of selling our goods on other markets by reaching agreements not only with the United Kingdom and with the commonwealth countries, not only with the European common market, but with all 15 NATO countries which are prepared to take and accept the necessary steps to help their industry.
I do not wish to pursue the matter any further, but I hope the minister will take the trouble to study the situation so that Canada may know where it is going and what it can expect.

When I replied on Friday to the minister's statement I chided him a bit for some omissions that occurred in his speech. After reading the Hansard record of Friday's debate I discovered that I myself made one or two serious omissions. I should like to take a few minutes now in order to repair those omissions, to avoid any misunderstanding that may arise and also to correct any wrong impression that may have been created.
Hon. members will recall that I compared the Minister of Trade and Commerce to a general who had called his troops in for a briefing to acquaint them with the facts of life of world trade. Among those facts of life in the world of trade I cited Russia's efforts to increase and accelerate her own industrial expansion while at the same time
[Mr. Caron.)
doing everything possible to hinder the industrial expansion of the free world.
I also referred to Russia's efforts to secure economic control of other countries and to integrate their economies into a trading bloc which would be complementary to her own. In addition I referred to Russia's economic aggression and penetration, and her increasing tendency to disrupt normal trading relations.
To counteract that action I made two suggestions. First I suggested that we should take action internally to protect ourselves against aggression and penetration and encourage other countries to do the same. I suggested that we should also take action externally to prevent trade disruption. In that connection I was thinking in terms of an association of free nations in the world of trade which would be somewhat similar to NATO in the realm of defence. Such an association would be able to buy up surpluses which Russia might use to disrupt world trade.
My first omission was the failure to point out that this in itself would not be enough, that what is actually needed is a dynamic, positive program, as was pointed out earlier this afternoon by my hon. friend from Ottawa West. The measures I was suggesting were by nature anti-communist, and I do not think there is any percentage in merely being anticommunist.
The military defeat of communism is something that cannot now be contemplated, and even were it possible, it would be useless because the evils that created communism would still remain. That is the real battle that has to be fought.
I think I pointed out to the minister last Friday some of the defects in our free enterprise system. I pointed out some of the weaknesses. Unfortunately these weaknesses are traceable to weaknesses in ourselves as human beings. If we are really going to do anything about this, we must come to grips with what is wrong in ourselves.
On Friday I spoke of the need for new goals. My second omission was the failure to call attention to what I consider should be our main goal at this time. That goal arises from a fact of life in the world of trade which is just as significant as the struggle for world domination in trade. This fact of life which I omitted is the gap in living standards between the industrialized countries and those countries we refer to as underdeveloped.
The people who live in the countries of Asia, India, Africa and other underdeveloped parts of the world, such as Latin America, have suddenly become increasingly aware of this gap. This has generated a wave of

nationalism in an effort to try and do something about it. They have before them examples of what Russia has accomplished in the space of 40 years. Even with the interruption of two world wars, we know that the Soviet union has developed from a backward nation to one of the foremost nations in the world as far as technological progress is concerned.
The people in these underdeveloped countries of Asia have another example in red China trying to achieve in 20 years what Russia achieved in 40 years. The industrial development of China is just as significant a fact in the world today as that of Russia.
In this connection Japan plays a very significant part. We know what it is to have on our borders a large trading nation. Japan is in exactly the same position and is experiencing the same pull economically as we are experiencing from the United States. Indeed, one of the main objectives of the policy of red China is to secure control of Japan in order to harness the industrial capacity of Japan to the manpower of China and the natural resources of southeast Asia. If China can succeed in doing this, she will outstrip the progress made by any nation in the world.
This afternoon the minister referred to Japan as an example of a nation which had risen from the ashes and had become one of our toughest competitors. This is of course true. However, we must not think of Japan only as a competitor. We must realize that Japan is also an ally of the free world and a key country in the survival of western democracy. Should the economy of Japan become dependent upon that of red China, the chances of survival for the free world would be very seriously impaired. Therefore, while we acknowledge Japan as a competitor we must conduct our trading relations with her as a country whose economy is vital to our own security.
The minister spoke this afternoon about the importance of design, quality and right prices. He said that if we paid attention to these matters we could achieve not only the second highest standard of living in the world, but even the highest standard of living. That is possibly true. However, I think there is the great danger that we might be tempted to make this our goal. If we did, we would do so at great peril to our survival as free peoples.
Certainly we must try and raise the living standards of people in our own country whose standards are still far below the national average; but to increase the over-all average of our standards of living in the western
Supply-Trade and Commerce world would serve only to increase the gap which exists between ourselves and these underdeveloped countries.
It is certainly in our interest that we should do everything possible to close that gap and assist the underdeveloped countries as quickly as possible. My colleague the hon. member for Ottawa West made that clear this afternoon. This is the goal at which I feel Canada and the free world should be aiming at this time and it is one of the things which I believe the minister should include in his briefing of his commissioners, businessmen, and all the contacts he makes as he attends trade conferences. It is a goal which all the people of Canada must be brought to accept. This is the kind of leadership which is required at this time. It is the kind of leadership that Canada could and should be giving in the world of trade, and I hope the minister will do everything in his power in that direction.

I do not wish to delay the passage of the first item on the minister's estimates but I have a few comments to make in connection with the conference of trade commissioners last fall and the subsequent action taken to complement that activity by the establishment of export credits.
I am wondering about the limiting factors in the operation of our trade commissioners, the obvious position being that the trade commissioners cannot in fact write an order on behalf of a particular manufacturer in Canada and in particular on behalf of the smaller secondary manufacturers. I am wondering, further, if any of the associations with which the minister has been dealing have evolved a method of sending abroad representatives of perhaps groups of industry within the same field or groups coming from a specified commercial area. I understand certain persons have given considerable thought to this and I wonder if the minister can tell us if he has encountered any efforts along these lines in his travels.
I wonder, too, if in approaching this problem of trade in the vigorous way in which the minister has approached it he has had the staff of his department examine specifically the procedures that were followed by Germany in the post-war years and in more recent years in developing the aggressive export trade pattern that they have evolved.
One other thought did occur to me, and I am wondering just how much consideration has been given to it, though perhaps it is being held in abeyance to await the impact and effect of the activities to date. I am wondering if something in the way of incentive has been considered in a broad or specific way to various industries which can

Supply-Trade and Commerce develop certain important increases either in our export trade generally or in certain selective areas.
X would appeciate very much hearing from the minister about these few matters.

In answer to the hon. member's questions, may I say that the board of trade for Vancouver send a trade mission overseas every year. This year they are sending a mission to Italy. Last year one went to Japan. I am advised that the Canadian chamber of commerce in 1959 sent a trade mission to the West Indies and that in 1960 they sent a trade mission to Australia and New Zealand. The Halifax board of trade recently sent a trade mission consisting of 128 persons for a two weeks trip to the United Kingdom and they have just returned from that market.
We are very happy indeed to co-operate closely with any chamber of commerce or board of trade that wishes to send missions overseas, or with any trade association. We encourage that very strongly. We make our trade commissioners available to them everywhere they would like to go, and this link between the department and these missions is a fruitful one indeed. It leads to directly increased trade and it enables people to go abroad in a group and develop trading opportunities.
Are these people qualified to write an order? That is the question which was in my mind. Are these people simply duplicating the activities of our trade commissioners?

The businessmen themselves must write the orders. There is nothing to stop a business firm appointing as an agent for the trip another businessman who happens to be going and telling him to accept or place orders under certain conditions. That could be done very easily, but it would be up to the individual firm to designate its own appointee.

Supposing a businessman
wanted to appoint a trade commissioner as an agent for a certain transaction, would he be precluded from doing that?

A trade commissioner could not enter into trade negotiations. He could do a tremendous amount of the preliminary work leading to a sale, but the actual signing of the contract must be done by the representative of the business itself.

I have very few words to say but they are of great importance to some of my constituents, as usual. I want to thank the minister for his replies to the questions I asked last Friday and tell him I am sorry I could not be here earlier this


afternoon to listen to the debate. My attendance was required at the external affairs committee to see that the affairs of the country were being run properly.
However, I do want to bring to the attention of the minister a question which I have raised in this chamber before. I have been asked by a number of my constituents to raise it again and then to make certain suggestions to the minister. The subject I have in mind is the unethical practices of a number of United States lumber and forest products industries particularly in the Kootenays in recent years. There have been 20 or more of these companies established. They operate for a year or so, show a profit in some cases and then owners or management disappear across the border while the employees, the creditors and others are left holding the bag.
The latest case involves the Hilco Lumber Company, Limited, near Fruitvale, British Columbia, whose activities I brought to the attention of the house on an earlier occasion. This company has been in operation for two or three years, and it succeeded in showing a profit of more than $43,000. In 1960 it ceased operations just prior to Christmas and showed total current liabilities of $141,893.46. Not only were the wages of employees unpaid for two or three months-some employees were owed up to $1,200-but a large number of business people had been defrauded. Provincial government assessments had been left unpaid. Money was owing in respect of the social service tax, the British Columbia property tax and other taxes.
There was, for example, the income tax deducted in respect of employees. The department is, I think, owed nearly $9,000. This money was deducted from the pay of employees and it belongs to the Department of National Kevenue. There are other taxes, accounts and so on owed all over the country. These men were left without a cent, and, to make it worse, when they went to collect their unemployment insurance they found that although this company had been operating for two or three years it had not paid a cent of unemployment insurance contributions. Here were these poor chaps left on the rocks without any entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits because the company had not purchased the stamps.
I understand that after a review of the circumstances had taken place provision was made for a considerable number of these men to receive unemployment benefits. I have received a good number of letters on this subject. The clergy of the churches of various denominations in the area have written to me, as have a number of other people, because they are aware of the circumstances

and of the plight caused to these employees by this dishonest management.
In addition to that I received a letter from a pioneer rancher who accumulated quite a large estate but who suffered the loss of a great many of his assets in recent years through the unethical practices in bankruptcy of the Wesley Lumber Company and the Ray Ragsdale Lumber Company. This is one illustration of what has happened at Golden, in areas along the Crowsnest Pass west of the Alberta border, around the Lardeau district, in the area of the upper Arrow Lakes, and in the Revelstoke area. This situation has become a blight in recent years. I want to emphasize the importance of this to the people in those areas concerned, as well as in other constituencies than mine. I was asked to take this matter up in the house and I have done so.

I thought the hon. member had finished. I was going to say that I am very interested in what he has said, and assure him that I will take this matter up very seriously. It does sound quite serious to me. I will discuss it with my appropriate colleagues to see if we can get to the bottom of this situation.

I appreciate the minister's co-operation and thank him for it. I intend to outline the story, but I will write the minister fully giving him photostat copies of the correspondence I have, as I am sure he is concerned with this situation.
The commercial attache to the United States embassy noticed some remarks which I made earlier this session, as they appeared in Hansard and, as a consequence, very kindly telephoned me stating that he was very disturbed about the situation and would do everything he could to assist. He has done that. An investigation was carried out in this regard. I will not deal with my correspondence with the commercial attache fully but will send copies to the minister. That individual has gone to considerable trouble instigating an investigation into the companies concerned in the United States. The results of that investigation are not of very much credit to the companies or individuals concerned.
I have also taken this matter up with the superintendent of bankruptcy who is also concerned with these repeated occurrences in my area as well as, I assume, other areas. I should suggest that these losses could be avoided with the co-operation of the department because they are occasioned by the lack of information and guidance. Honourable people living in isolated spots, not used to consulting lawyers or bankers, witness a man driving a Cadillac-this did happen on one occasion-spending a few thousand dollars
Supply-Trade and Commerce for a week or so and think he is a millionaire. I am not as easily taken in as some individuals in my constituency have been. I would suggest that perhaps the minister should look at the situation and, with the co-operation of other departments and the commercial attache to the United States embassy, who I am sure is very willing to co-operate, could supply the information in order to curb this rash of fraudulent operations in bankruptcy. Perhaps an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act, will be required.
The superintendent of bankruptcy wrote me a letter dated April 21, 1961 from which I would like to quote a paragraph which reads as follows:
However, unfortunately, the Bankruptcy Act as now constituted does not seem to contain a remedy and I must confess that the solution is not immediately apparent. Should you have any suggestions, I shall be only too pleased to receive them and to give them due and proper consideration in conjunction with a study of the present provisions.
While it may be possible to amend the Bankruptcy Act so as to have stricter control over these things, I am of the opinion that the most effective approach must be made through the minister's department, with the assistance of the commercial attache to the United States embassy. I urge the minister to give this his consideration, to see what can be done either by distributing information to various organizations, such as the chambers of commerce and farmers' bodies, advising them of the steps that can be taken, or perhaps by an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act. I shall be very pleased to assist the minister in any way I can and give him any information I have in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very glad to look into the matter as soon as I receive that information from the hon. member.

I also believe that it would be well for our chambers of commerce and trade unions to promote a "Buy Canadian" campaign.
Such an attitude would allow our economy to recover its strength, as it is only normal that Canadian products be first absorbed by those who manufacture them and by the taxpayers of this country.
As the minister stated this afternoon-and I think it bears repeating-some countries which formerly, and more particularly during the war, were among our customers, have in the last two years become our competitors. That is our position now. To my mind, the best way of settling the issue would be to compete in the most efficient manner with those who were formerly among our best customers. Those countries have conquered markets we would like to have ourselves.

I am particularly interested in the lumber and mining industries in my area, both of which reached and receded from their peak some years ago. Towns like Kirkland Lake are faced each year with a loss of another mine and the income derived from it. We regard with envy Toronto and some of the other major cities that are situated close to the markets for their products because while we are losing our resources these areas are overexpanding until it has become detrimental to many of the people who live there. It seems unrealistic to me that a person has to get up three or four hours before he is to start work and drive for two or three hours to get to his place of employment when we in other parts of the country have facilities very close at hand and would welcome plants that could be located almost in the backyard of the employees' residential areas.
It seems to me that we are going to have to do in Canada what has been done in other countries. I should like to refer to Great Britain as an example. I am told that recently when the Ford Motor Company asked for permission to expand in the location in which they were then situated they were told that they would be given a permit to expand but their expansion would have to take place in Liverpool because Liverpool had a surplus of labour and it was advantageous to have the new development carried out in that area.
I suggest that this is the type of development we need in Canada. There should be some leadership from the Department of Trade and Commerce in the establishing of secondary industry in those areas where there is now none and will not be unless there is government intervention, either through rendering assistance in the form of a subsidy
[Mr. Peters !

or in the form of direction by telling a company that it cannot have a licence to establish a plant in a certain town because the government wants the company to establish it in another town. The company could be told that it would be given a licence and encouragement to establish in the other town. If this is done, we will be able to share the wealth, so to speak, much more evenly than at the present time.
I should like to use the example of the town of Matachewan in my riding. No doubt many members of the Conservative party were interested in the past in the stocks of mines such as Young Davidson, Matachewan Consolidated and other producing mines in that area. The town has four or five grocery stores, a couple of drug stores, a small hardware store, a police station, a fire brigade and two or three schools, but the facilities available are not now being used. The town does not even have the money to pay for caretakers for some of the public buildings. The town is bankrupt for the simple reason that there is no industry there.
It seems rather unreasonable that new factories should be allowed to locate in a high wage area such as Toronto where agricultural lands are being taken over for the building of homes. There are many reasons why that also should not take place, but people are living so far away from where they work that in some cases the situation is becoming ridiculous. Yet this is happening while at the same time a municipality such as Matachewan will provide free land for the establishment of industries and will make every reasonable concession, tax or otherwise, to get firms to establish factories there. There are many natural resources in the area of Matachewan that would lend themselves to the establishment of secondary industry. The authorities there will grant every reasonable consideration just to get an industry to establish there so that the people of the area will again be employed and will be able to maintain their community in a reasonable degree of prosperity.
I think it is not unreasonable to ask that the small business bureau of the Department of Trade and Commerce undertake such a program in conjunction with what it is now doing because in my opinion it is going to be vitally necessary. The junior member for Halifax, who is parliamentary secretary to the minister, has a somewhat similar situation in the area he represents. We continually hear complaints from the maritimes that they have a problem quite similar to the one to which I have referred in connection with

northern Ontario. As one of his colleagues has mentioned, assistance is going to have to be given.
Progress reported.
